maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEES OF THE WHOLE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEES OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the house will learn with deep regret of the serious illness of the hon. member for Spa-dina OMr. Rea), who for a considerable period of time has occupied the position of deputy chairman of committees of the whole house. In view of his inability to discharge the responsibilities of his position his wife, speaking for him, has asked that some hon. member be appointed in his place. I am sure that hon. members generally join with me in a tribute to his ability and the fairness with which he discharged his duties, coupled with the hope that in the not too distant future he may return to the house again.
In order to carry on the business of the house a successor must be appointed, and I suggest the name of Gordon Chown, the member for Winnipeg South. From time to time he has occupied the chair as chairman of the committee of the whole, and the reaction of hon. members generally is indicative of the fact that in the discharge of that position he has acted with ability and fairness. Since coming to the house in 1957 he has made a careful study of the rules and has also become imbued with the traditions of parliament. I believe that if the house agrees to his appointment he will fill the position with dignity and restraint.
I therefore move, seconded by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill): That Gordon Campbell Chown, Esquire, member for the electoral district of Winnipeg South, be appointed deputy chairman of committees of the whole house in the place of Charles Edward Rea, Esquire, member for the electoral district of Spadina, who is unable to carry on his duties because of illness.

House of Commons

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEES OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is approved I should like to join with the Prime Minister in expressing the grief that we on this side of the house feel because of the fact that the hon. member for Spadina is unable to carry on his duties as deputy chairman of committees of the whole house. I should like to say on our behalf that we have admired the manner in which he has implemented and put into effect the rules of the house. We have found him to be extremely fair, and we will regret his absence from the post which he held. We trust that his illness will be temporary, and that he will be able to resume his duties in the not too distant future.
I should also like to join with the Prime Minister in supporting to the fullest extent the motion he has just made for the appointment of the hon. member for Winnipeg South. We have seen the hon. member for Winnipeg South in action on more than one occasion, and I am sure I express the views of members on this side of the house when I say that he is moved by one object and one object alone, to see that the rules of the house are applied with fairness and with equity. There is no doubt in our minds that he attempts at all times to be objective in his interpretation of the rules of the house, and that is why we are happy to support this motion.

subtopic: EXPORT OF UNLOADING PUMPS

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, yesterday I told the house of the action which the government was taking to ensure that grain shipments to mainland China would not be interrupted or delayed by the problem which had arisen over United States unloading equipment. At that time I indicated that in addition to the urgent steps which were being taken to investigate or develop alternative sources of supply, the Canadian ambassador in Washington was discussing the matter at senior levels of the United States administration. I explained that while the decision was within the jurisdiction of the United States government, the government of Canada was urging a review of the earlier ruling which had abruptly cut off delivery of these necessary pieces of equipment.
As a result of the prompt and careful attention which this problem received in Washington yesterday, the United States treasury department is now prepared, as an exceptional measure, to license United States corporations, if they apply, to export grain unloading equipment already on order for installation on ships delivering grain from Canadian ports under charter to communist China.
Although this relaxation is limited to equipment which has already been ordered, I understand that the orders so far placed are likely to take care of the immediate requirements and enable full scale loading to proceed without difficulty over at least the next few weeks while deliveries of pumps from other sources are being arranged by those operators whose ships will arrive later and whose requirements may not be already covered by orders.
The United States authorities took this decision at the request of the Canadian government. I am sure that hon. members generally would want to say how much we appreciate the good sense which the United States administration has shown in reconsidering this matter of concern to Canada. The adjustments which they have made have not been easy for them in the light of the long established policies in their country and the strong feelings regarding any United States participation in trade with communist China. This is a further evidence of the relations between our countries whereby each

country, without in any way derogating from its own sovereignty or independence, endeavours by diplomatic means to accommodate the other. Such co-operation is an example to all the world.

subtopic: EXPORT OF UNLOADING PUMPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to join, and join wholeheartedly, with the Prime Minister in what he has just said about this example of the kind of co-operation which is the result of a long history of good neighbourliness between Canada and the United States, a good neighbourliness that is fostered by attempts always to understand, always to deal with the facts and always to avoid exacerbating differences which from time to time obviously will arise.

subtopic: EXPORT OF UNLOADING PUMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased with the announcement the Prime Minister has been able to make this morning. We think the initial action that was taken was in error and was a mistake. We are pleased that this has now been corrected and that the pumps in question will be made available for the speedy shipment of this grain to China.
I want to congratulate the Prime Minister for having taken prompt and resolute action on this particular occasion.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres asked me a question concerning action taken by customs officials with respect to a quantity of goods destined for Cuba.
In reply I wish to state that under the Export and Import Permits Act, an export permit is required in connection with the

re-export of goods originating outside Canada. I should like to refer to my statement in this house on December 16, 1960, which may be found on page 867 of Hansard for that date. I concluded that statement by saying:
As the Prime Minister has also stated, there is no intention of permitting what, in effect, would amount to bootlegging of goods of United States origin to Cuba. To implement this policy, no permits will be issued for the re-export of United States origin goods to Cuba.
In the present case it appeared to the customs officials that the shipment in question included goods originating outside Canada. It also appeared to these officials that no export permit had been issued in connection with the goods. Furthermore, the export entry form indicated that the goods were not of foreign origin. As a result of the possibility that there was a violation of the Export and Import Permits Act or the Customs Act, or both, the goods were held for further investigation.
The shipment in question involves 165 cases of a variety of industrial equipment. At this time detailed information regarding the individual products cannot be disclosed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Defence Production arising out of a statement made by the minister on June 6, to the effect that the Canadian government will undertake the development of a snow vehicle for the United States army. Mr. Speaker, I had several plants in mind, but the United States government had one particular plant in mind only. I think perhaps I should give the following statement to the house.
After exhaustive examination of the proposals from Canadian industry, the United States army selected the Canadair vehicle as the one which came closest to meeting its requirements. Contract negotiations are now under way with the department and the United States army, and it is expected that we shall put forward a recommendation concerning this contract within the next three weeks. It is expected that if this contract goes well there could be large production quantities ordered.
The CL 91 is a small amphibious articulated tracked vehicle with high off-road mobility, and is capable of carrying a one ton payload or a light infantry section. The front unit or utility carrier portion of the CL 91 can

The recommendation of the United States army is to negotiate the development project with Canadair.

speechtext: This item will be found on page 75 of the blue book and the details on page 520.

Mr. Chairman, it is a unique privilege for me to make the first remarks while you preside over our destinies as deputy chairman of the committee of the whole house. We who heard your words a few moments ago know that you will indeed bring to this exacting position all the qualities of heart and mind that will enable you to successfully follow the distinguished pattern set by your predecessor, the hon. member for Spadina.
Sir, one of the disadvantages in speaking in a debate which in effect has been trifurcated and been before the house on at least three different occasions-this is perhaps the fourth or even fifth-is that sometimes the trails grow cold and one does not have the opportunity for some weeks really to reply to some contentious remarks.
I refer to a remark made by the hon. member for Port Arthur concerning winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river. I should like

Supply-Transport
to deal with what he said later. First, sir, I should like to turn to a rather prosaic and humble matter, yet one that is of some importance to me. It concerns the working hours of cooks on Department of Transport vessels on the east coast. As found on page 5918 of Hansard there is a rather lengthy reply, filed by the minister, to questions of mine concerning the working conditions and wages of cooks, stewards and other crew on departmental ships on both the east and west coasts. I may say that I have also had replies on the same subject from the Department of Mines and Technical Survey and the Department of Fisheries, and respecting civilian manned auxiliary vessels of the Department of National Defence.
In each and every instance cooks and stewards on the east coast work 48 hours per week, while the working week for everybody else, other crew on the east coast and cooks, stewards and other crew on the west coast, is only 40 hours. This was not always so. I understand that until a few years ago cooks and stewards had the same hours of work as other crew, but that the Department of Labour, in making a prevailing rate survey, found that on smaller non-governmental vessels cooks did work these longer hours and so the government cooks were bounced back to the 48-hour week.
I suggest to the Minister of Transport and to the other ministers concerned that this is most unjust. In the first place, I do not think you can have a happy ship when the arrangements respecting working hours are divided in this way so that one group has to work longer than other members of the ship's crew. I suggest further that the prevailing rate formula needs thorough investigation and re-examination in this instance, for it seems to me that there are probably more cooks and stewards employed on the vessels of the four departments I have mentioned than are employed on non-governmental ships operating on the east coast. Perhaps I am wrong in that view, but if I am right then in effect the working conditions for these cooks and stewards are being fashioned in much the same way as if the working conditions of a man in a very large restaurant were determined by what was applicable in the case of the short order cook in the hot dog stand right next door.
As I say, this seems to me a very unjust situation, and I ask not only the Minister of Transport but also his colleagues the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Fisheries to correct it.
May I turn next to the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier, who on May 20 was good enough to devote some of his comments to

the Canadian institute of communications. We in the institute would like to say to him how very much we appreciate this first mention in the House of Commons of this brand new baby on the Canadian communication scene. The hon. member for Laurier suggested that the Department of Transport make a contribution to our institute under the item in the estimates dealing with membership in international organizations. We welcome his suggestion and his interest, but I have talked this matter over with some of my fellow directors, and while no final decision has been reached as yet we would ask that the request or the suggestion be held in abeyance until we have had an opportunity to discuss it further.
I would, however, ask the Minister of Transport on behalf of the other directors of the Canadian institute of communications if he would encourage senior officials of his department to become members of our institute. Our reluctance to come forward at this time is simply that we wish to retain as much independence for our institute as we possibly can. I do not wish to appear to be speaking in a fashion derogatory of parliament or of the government, but at the same time some of us have doubts about the wisdom of encouraging a large government contribution. However, we shall be presenting our views to the minister and, since the hon. member for Laurier was good enough to raise the matter, we shall keep him in touch with the picture as well.
A third matter is this. For some years it has been very difficult in the Atlantic coast area of the maritimes to obtain accurate weather forecasts. Perhaps the most famous instance in recent years arose, I think it was, on New Year's eve when the forecast had predicted a few snow flurries and all of a sudden we were whacked in the Halifax area with over 20 inches of snow. One can conjure up in one's mind the riotous picture of what a sudden 20 inch snowfall can do to driving conditions on a New Year's eve, when even under the best possible weather conditions driving is apt to be tricky.
There is a reason why the weather forecasters in Halifax have experienced these difficulties. It is not because of any lack of ability or training on the part of the staff. I can assure the minister of that; they are fine people. The difficulty is that much of our maritime weather comes from off the Atlantic ocean. It is true that many weather masses move across the continent to the maritimes, and these can be accurately charted all the way. The difficulty we have experienced arises out of unexpected weather developments coming from the gulf stream or over parts of the Atlantic ocean.

I am happy to see from the estimates that between $140,000 and $150,000 has been provided by the department to set up what is known as a weather radar station. Perhaps I may explain what that is in simple and non-technical terms. An ordinary radar station screens out the weather factors in front of it and picks out objects. The weather radar station for which, I understand, tenders will shortly be called, eliminates solid objects in front of the screen and picks out the weather factors. One could almost visualize it in terms of the positive and negative of a photograph, although that is not an exact parallel. In any event, the system should do much to improve our weather forecasting and, maybe, even our chance of getting home safely on New Year's eve.
The final point I should like to make has reference to some remarks by the hon. member for Port Arthur when he took part in this debate on May 13. Perhaps I can quote the paragraph with which I intend to take issue. As reported at the bottom of the second column of page 4773 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
We know that there are now icebreakers and mechanical devices which can keep the port of Montreal open for almost the whole of the year. We also know that this is a delicate political problem because it is going to have its repercussions and its effects upon Halifax and Saint John. Yet I had a figure given to me by a man who is very prominent in shipping. He pointed out to me that the average saving per ton on freight coming through Halifax and Saint John in the winter as against that coming through Montreal is $12 a ton in favour of Montreal. One only has to look at the amount of freight coming through the two maritime ports in order to realize that we are in effect subsidizing the Atlantic ports by not pushing very strongly a policy to open up Montreal to winter shipping.
The hon. member for Port Arthur has made a fundamental error in stating the problem so simply. If there were to be shipping to Montreal throughout the winter an extra cost would be involved, a cost which I do not think the hon. member has taken into his calculations. This would be the cost of providing extra special icebreaking services up the St. Lawrence river to Montreal; and no one who has seen that river frozen over in winter fails to realize that it would be a herculean task to clear that ice aside. The cost of such an operation would, I suggest, be fabulous and out of this world.
On the other hand, the ports of Halifax and Saint John are free of ice the year round. If the hon. member for Port Arthur had said that it would be legitimate to heap on the cost of this special icebreaking service, or if he had taken that into account when discussing this matter with his friend who gave him that advice, I think he would have found
Supply-Transport
that the competitive advantages would more than favour Halifax and Saint John.
I am personally not one who stands against progress of the kind that is argued here, but if we are going to need extra services provided by icebreakers-and these would be more costly icebreakers than the ones we have in operation now-it would be only fair to add the cost of the service to the shipping charges. Then we would see who is competitive and who is non-competitive, or who is being subsidized and who is not being subsidized.
May I present, very briefly, the point of view on this tricky question which was expressed by the port of Halifax commission. There are six points made concerning this matter and I shall list them quickly. They are taken from a brief presented to the minister on winter navigation in the St. Lawrence river.
In our opinion, therefore, icebreaker activity in the St. Lawrence river and gulf should be limited to:
(a)	Anti-flooding operations;
(b)	Assisting Canadian coastal shipping and ferries;
(c)	Assisting any kind of vessel in the gulf;
(d)	Assisting, but not beyond Quebec city on the upriver voyage, nor before Quebec city on the downriver voyage, vessels engaged in international trade which are shown in Lloyds register of shipping as "ice reinforced";
(e)	Ice reinforced vessels should pay for icebreaker service at a price which would be reasonable for such service on a commercial basis;
(f)	However, if the above are not to produce situations contrary to government policy as outlined above, and most harmful to Canadian Atlantic ports, the river must be closed between certain specific dates during the winter season to all vessels engaged in international trade other than those mentioned at (d) above.
Perhaps with regard to that last recommendation I do not go as far as some of my maritime colleagues. I think the present policy of the government is satisfactory, namely that the icebreaking service should be provided to vessels which are reinforced against ice. In other words, it helps vessels which have a proper reason for being in the river when ice conditions are difficult or when, for unexpected reasons, the ice may get out of hand. On the other hand it does not give carte blanche to any tramp steamer or freighter not adequately equipped to deal with ice to be in areas where severe ice conditions are expected. I think that is a reasonable policy, but in order to ensure that the maritime view is fully presented I thought I might quote from the brief which, I understand, has already been sent to the Minister of Transport.

I shall refer later to the icebreaking situation in the St. Lawrence river, but I wish first of all to draw attention to a question which I know is puzzling members

Supply-Transport
of this house, and that is the complete inability of the Minister of Transport to give us any indication when a properly constituted committee of this house is going to meet and have before it the officials of the Canadian National Railways.
We know that the president of the C.N.R. and his officials cannot be completely at the disposal of the whims of any House of Commons committee. We know that the minister is our means of liaison with the railway company, and that it is through the minister the arrangements will be made. The committee has not yet met. No chairman has been selected. We are not under way. But the very failure to go ahead and bring Mr. Gordon before the committee or to see that he comes before the committee is leading to speculation of a kind which I think is regrettable.
I know it is being argued that one of the reasons Mr. Gordon is not before the committee is that he has said he will not come until his position as chairman of the board has been cleared up. I dismiss this story, but it is the kind of thing we shall be hearing until we know more definitely when the affairs of the C.N.R. are to be examined. I think it is time the minister let us know definitely and concretely when Mr. Gordon is to appear, because the committee cannot decide until it hears through its pipe line to the president, and the minister is that pipe line. I think it is time he let us know when this meeting is going to take place.
We hear all kinds of speculation about when this session is going to adjourn or when it is going to end. We are chivvied in certain places and told we must rush to get out committee reports because this session is going to adjourn at the end of June, and perhaps it is going to end on that date.
All I know is that it is now the 8th day of June. There is not very much time left and we have this important committee coming up. It was agreed that this year the affairs of the C.N.R. and the T.C.A. would be separated, that there would be time for reflection and consideration. The minister is aware that there is unusual interest in the C.N.R. this year and that the study of its affairs is going to take more time, one would judge, than in previous years. I think it is most unfortunate and unfair that we have not been given a date for the meeting of that committee.
One of the arguments which is always put before us when Mr. Gordon comes here is that we cannot tie up the C.N.R. for too long, and it is therefore necessary to meet at 10 in the morning and sit right through until late at night, sometimes 10 o'clock. This procedure certainly has some advantages in enabling us to hasten through the report of the C.N.R., 
but it has marked disadvantages for the members of the committee who are trying to marshall the kind of thorough analysis they wish to make.
I wish to draw to the attention of the minister in this regard the fact that the committee on broadcasting has had before it another government corporation, the C.B.C., for weeks on end. For at least two days and sometimes three days a week we have had the president and the senior officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation before us and somehow, although, I am sure at a great disadvantage, the C.B.C. has managed to keep functioning.
I just want the minister to note the difference between treatment we give to the executives of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the treatment we give to the head of the Canadian National Railways. The committee on broadcasting has Mr. Ouimet before it in the morning or perhaps in morning and afternoon sittings. Then there is a break for several days. Mr. Gordon has never had that kind of treatment, nor have other presidents of the Canadian National Railways. Yet I suggest there is not that much difference in the role of the corporation in terms of public interest and in terms of the interest of members of parliament.
I would hope that this year we could make some arrangement whereby the committee before which the C.N.R. appears is more slowly paced so that, when it meets, we can do a decent and thorough job. I would not go so far as to suggest that we should use the C.B.C. treatment as a model, but I do suggest that something more on that line would be better than this tremendous emphasis we have in the sessional committee on railways and shipping to drive through and get it all over with.
I think the minister is aware of the fact that a committee can sometimes operate much better if it has a bit of opportunity to consider the evidence rather than have it come before it in something of a staccato fashion. If you take an analogy in sports, it seems to me that it is much easier to watch a football game or a baseball game than it is to watch a hockey game, because you have more pauses and more chance to reflect on what is going on. It is one straight hockey game when Donald Gordon appears before us, with no periods called and really no offsides. I hope the minister will give consideration to that matter and let us know where we stand on the Donald Gordon situation. When is he coming?
The next point I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister is something I touched on last year, namely the rather unusual growth in the Department of Transport. At that time I pointed out to hon. members

who represent free enterprise in this chamber that one of the consequences of some of the peculiar actions in the non-free enterprise sphere of this government is that more and more responsibilities are being put upon the Department of Transport and that it is growing in size. Even someone like myself who is not a forthright free enterpriser cannot help but be concerned about the growth in size of the Department of Transport.
I would ask the minister this question. Can he give us a projection in respect of air services, which seems to represent the fastest growing part of his deparment? Can he give us a projection for the next five years with regard to the numbers of people who are going to be employed? We have had prefigured for us on a number of occasions an astounding line of expenditures for air services in all aspects. It seems to me that we should get some idea of how big the growth is going to be in terms of personnel. It seems to me that this would be fair information.
The other thing that I wanted to ask in relation to personnel is this. Will the minister explain why, in reducing the amount of information provided in the annual report, it has been decided to dispense with the information on employees and the relative places of their employment? This seems to me to be among the useful information that was in the report. If any hon. members feel that I am carping at what may have been done to save money, I should like them to compare the report we get in relation to penitentiaries and the one we get in relation to the Department of Transport. In the one report we are just blown over with figures and details, even about the meals in one small reform institution. Here we have the fastest growing department in the government and its report gets smaller, less detailed and less informative every year.
Before I sit down I should like to touch on the point raised by the hon. member for Halifax, who indicated that I had made one fundamental error in my remarks on the icebreaking possibilities in the St. Lawrence in connection with the advantages that Montreal had in terms of $12 a ton over freight costs vis-a-vis Halifax and Saint John. I did not raise that matter in order to suggest that Saint John or Halifax should be forgotten. I quite agree that the cost of the icebreaking service should be taken into consideration. However, if we wish to move toward a stage where our transportation services in this country are based upon a service principle and the lowest possible cost to the shipper-and this seems to me to be the ideal, whether it is a public service providing them or whether it is a private service
Supply-Transport
providing them-we need to know more about the relative costs of shipping and of using various ports and various alternatives.
Despite what the hon. member for Halifax read from the brief of the Halifax people expressing their views, I think the hon. member is also aware of the fact that along the Gulf of St. Lawrence and in Montreal there are groups that have contradictory views. I am not suggesting that one group should be heard and another should not be heard. I am suggesting that the job of the Department of Transport is to determine what will give us the most efficient, and the cheapest and the best service, and that somehow we should have a resolution of this problem. Since it will continue to be a political problem in resolving the naturally selfish interests of Montreal and its shippers against the naturally selfish interests in those terms of the cities of Halifax and Saint John, it is not going to be an easy one to solve. However, it seems to me that some attempt should be gotten under way to tackle problems such as this.
The hon. member for Peterborough is going to make some suggestions in this regard as to how we should work toward solving some of these fundamental problems in transportation where we have a choice and where, whatever choice is made, someone is going to get hurt. However, the point is that if we do not make the choice or turn toward the principle of efficient and fair service, we are going to continue to carry the extra burden in transportation costs about which we all complain and which was the subject of so much repetition before the royal commission on transportation.
As I close my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I am very pleased that you have attained your post. When I heard that you were going to have a permanent senior position I of course immediately thought back to last Thursday, I think it was, when you were acting chairman and I was ruled out of order. At the time I had a fairly good case. However, I recognize the fact that there was nothing personal or partisan about your decision. I just hope that you will have as good a time in the post as your predecessor had. I also hope-and I am not saying this as any reflection on you-that you will gain the affection that your predecessor had with almost everyone I have encountered in the House of Commons. I would say without reservation that I personally have never encountered in this House of Commons a more popular member or better liked person than your predecessor in the post. In this sense it seems to me both our sympathy and

Supply-Transport
our co-operation must go out to you, because you have a real job before you in filling that role.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am prompted to rise at this time, Mr. Chairman, because of some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur. But prior to dealing with them may I say that I think the minister should clarify the position created by a statement made in the other place by the president of the national Progressive Conservative association, when he suggested that the management and the administration of the Canadian National Railways should be split into two divisions, or in other words that there should be an administrative head and a chairman of the board.
I think the committee is entitled to know here and now, before this item goes through, what is the position of the government in respect to this matter. After all, this is of considerable importance to the house and to the country. Here is what the Ottawa Journal, whose sympathies toward the government are well known, had to say in an editorial which appeared on June 5 entitled: Mr. Gordon and the C.N.R.
I should just like to quote a portion of it:
The Senate has heard a suggestion from one of its members that Mr. Donald Gordon be relieved of his duties as chairman of the board of the C.N.R. so that he, Mr. Gordon, might concentrate on the running of the railroad, either as president or general manager.
This suggestion lacks not only wisdom but decision.
It presumably wants to remove Mr. Gordon from the control of the C.N.R. but doesn't say so in so many words. It fiddles about with the titles but is not forthright. Thus it lacks decision.
It assumes that this is a time when our national railway can be put under a kind of two-headed leadership, one of whom would perhaps be receptive to suggestions from Ottawa and the other (Mr. Gordon) would be receptive to nothing but his own judgment of the merits of any given case. Thus it lacks wisdom.
Because of the last paragraph of this editorial I am going to put the whole of it on the record. It goes on to say:
The Journal is not so naive as to imagine that the life of a government is easy when it is trying to deal with a man like Donald Gordon, whether in wartime price controls or peacetime running of a railroad. Mr. Gordon is a large and independent man, messenger for no one. Such a man may not always be right, may not suffer politicians gladly. But such a man is more likely to be a successful head of a national railroad in these strenuous and revolutionary times than some chairman of the board with smooth manners and soft convictions.
That is an editorial which the minister might well ponder before he and his colleagues in the government make a decision on this matter. However, in view of what has been said by the hon. member for Port

Arthur I say to the minister that it would be absolutely wrong and a serious mistake to call the president of the Canadian National Railways here as a witness before the committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and operated by the government until his position is clarified by the government.
Not only do I think it is unfair, but I think it is immoral on the part of the government to continue the present situation as it has been since September of last year. Here is the president of a great national railway who, together with three of his co-directors, does not know what his position is. Not only is it ungrateful; it is disgraceful on the part of the government to hold up a matter of this importance in the manner in which it has been held up.
The legislation dealing with the directors of the Canadian National Railways passed through this house and I understand it has now passed the other place, or is about to be reported upon if it has not already gone through the other place. If that is the case there should be no further hesitation on the part of the government in making known its position.
I do not think it would be fair to those who are responsible for the administration of this great railway, particularly the president, to call Mr. Gordon before the committee unless and until his position is made clear and he knows whether or not he is going to be carrying on as president of the railway.

Mr. Chairman, may I join other hon. members who have congratulated you on what is really the confirmation of your appointment. We have already seen the manner in which you conduct the committees of this house. We know you will live up to the standard set by your predecessor who, as the hon. member for Port Arthur stated, is a very respected and greatly loved member of this house. I would only say, sir, that in the course of the business we have already conducted in the present session you have certainly given every indication that the committees of the house will be conducted in accordance with the highest traditions of parliament.
May I say to the Minister of Transport, in the same respect, how much we appreciate the co-operation which he has shown, in particular to private members, in dealing with matters related to his department.
I want to make one or two what may appear to be slightly disjointed comments because of the relatively large area of administration which comes under the supervision or within the purview of the minister. I do not intend to enlarge on these matters because they are problems which are well known to the minister. However, I suggest that in his

reply the minister might make some reference to the points I raise, because I know it is not necessary to take up the time of the committee in providing the background, much of which has already been introduced into this debate.
We have had several royal commissions examining the problems of various aspects of transportation. The one currently sitting, dealing with railway transportation, has already recognized the various factors involved, such as competition with other forms of transportation in Canada. I think it is safe to say that the competition of air transportation with the railways will increase to such a point that the day may well come when, because of the progress in air transportation, we will find we have literally relegated the railways to being low grade haulers. I say this because quite obviously the competition which has been experienced in other areas of the world both in air freight and air passenger services has had a similar effect on railway companies in the countries concerned. I think this is generally recognized.
I have listened with some interest to the many criticisms of the president of the C.N.R. I think it is perhaps fair to say that some of these criticisms are based on fact, but I hope no hon. member of this committee will assume that because there is a substantial deficit in the C.N.R. the responsibility should, in effect, be borne solely by the president of the railway. I need not defend this gentleman, because he is well able to defend himself. However, I would point out that there seems to be an inclination on the part of some hon. members to hold the president of the railway entirely responsible for the difficulty in which this railway finds itself.
This brings me to the point that I want to make very clear. I think the minister has perhaps one of the greatest responsibilities of any member of the cabinet. We are already well aware of the advances made in aviation in Canada, and the history and tradition we have in this respect are second to none in the world. However, it is not enough just to sit back and assume that we have done enough in the field of aviation because we have been successful in developing efficient air line services and, to some degree, freight services; because we were successful in developing a commonwealth flying program during the emergency years, the first 2i years of the war, or because we have successfully pioneered much of the north country through aviation.
I feel that some people in Canada-and I am not speaking specifically of those in government-have been inclined to sit back and say that we can let matters take their course; that we can share in the progress of aviation
Supply-Transport
in the future without putting in all our imagination and all our effort to see that we continue to advance in this field.
Therefore I say to the minister that I think his responsibility within the department is greater in this field than that of any other person in Canada, and he has a duty to see that Canada is kept ahead in every aspect of aviation. His responsibility is not limited to the providing of assistance through a crown company, or private industry. I suggest that his responsibility includes the carrying out of regular surveys in regard to the possibility of increasing our air freight and passenger transportation through the negotiation of bilateral agreements with other countries so as to provide a greater opportunity for our air carriers to compete in the international field.
I think there is an additional responsibility on the part of the minister in respect to the equipment which Canadian carriers are using today both in air freight and air passenger services. There exist in Canada two very competent manufacturers of aircraft equipment. I think hon. members of this house will remember at least some of the history in this regard, which shows that at one time it was possible to provide one of our air lines with Canadian made aircraft. I suggest to the minister that, in co-operation with the two principal carriers, he should consider the possibility of determining whether these carriers could be provided with Canadian aircraft built in Canada, to be utilized in their passenger and air freight services. I suggest that one of the two aircraft manufacturers has already developed suitable aircraft for exactly this purpose, and I believe the other company is equally capable of doing so. If this were accomplished we should not have to depend on any other source for these aircraft.
In terms of aviation, I suggest we cannot neglect the civilian side of air development, nor can we overlook the contribution which it makes. I refer specifically to the royal Canadian flying clubs. I think it is an historical fact that these clubs contributed, perhaps more than any other element of aviation, to the success of the commonwealth training program to which I have already referred. It is equally true that some two years ago the Department of National Defence withdrew its financial support of those flying clubs. I presume this withdrawal can be justified by the fact that the air force is, to a large degree, training its own pilots. However, I suggest it is equally important that we consider the difficulties with which the flying clubs are currently attempting to cope in order to continue their operations.
These problems fall roughly into two categories. The first category involves excessive

Supply-Transport
ground rate rentals which are being charged by the Department of Transport. The second category arises from the fact that many of the clubs have had to face increased costs for their facilities. These were previously provided at a rather nominal rental rate. Following the war, however, crown assets corporation was asked to dispose of them, with priority, of course, given to the flying clubs, but at considerable cost.
These non-profit organizations have little hope of survival in many instances because of the two factors I have referred to. I think we can also add to those two factors the knowledge that high municipal assessments and tax rates have, in part, created the financial burden of these clubs. Many of them are now in very serious financial difficulties. Quite obviously the department cannot be expected to assume the entire responsibility for the success of civil aviation in this field. Nevertheless, I suggest that the minister and his colleagues should review the situation very carefully regarding the future of civil aviation in Canada, in terms of what might still be expected in the way of providing pilots, because we dare not underestimate the part that civil aviation will continue to play in the whole aviation picture. I think it is fair to say that in certain areas this element of aviation will provide service to commercial air lines, and to some degree to the air force in Canada. I think it is important that it be remembered that a great many young men are being trained by those flying clubs and, therefore, the government has a major responsibility.
So, I should like to ask the minister to comment in regard to my observations, and to perhaps review very carefully the financial contributions which the government makes in an attempt to maintain the position of the royal Canadian flying clubs.
In this respect I have a second suggestion to make to the minister. There exists in the United States a body known as the civil air patrol, which is to a very large extent a military organization. It also involves civil pilots, and as a result is a rather unique organization. Today in Canada we are concerned with civil defence to perhaps a greater degree than at any other time in our history. I suggest that the minister, in co-operation with his colleague the Minister of National Defence, should make a close examination of the part that civil aviation can again play in the development of a more effective civil air patrol in Canada. Such a body does exist now. I suggest we could utilize a vast armada of aircraft, in the event of an emergency, to supplement the civil defence activity within this country. I suggest this is a broad field

in which, largely through organizational responsibility, the minister, together with his colleague the Minister of National Defence, could again make a very important contribution.
Another aspect of the subject of civil aviation involves the location of the fields which are in current use. I think it is a fact that many of us are concerned because the municipal fields, and those fields operated by the department, are becoming somewhat overcrowded. I feel the experience the United States has had in the past few years clearly indicates the necessity of a major change by wherever possible removing civil aviation operation from those areas of commercial operation. This necessity is borne out by the fact that where there is an active air field used by civil, domestic and international air lines, the risk of accident is extreme. Almost every year a number of R.C.A.F. air fields are declared surplus because of the decrease in activity at those particular fields. I suggest to the minister, therefore, that he might give us his own view, and the views of his department, regarding the development of auxiliary fields for the use of private aviation in Canada. I suggest that would first of all provide a greater safety factor to air passengers, and, second, would provide much more orderly development of civil aviation in Canada.
My final comment deals with the important question of international and domestic competition between the Canadian air carriers. I think this subject has been adequately covered by a number of hon. members who have spoken before me, but I should like to say to the minister that he will soon have to face that problem or one of our air carriers, because of the restrictions imposed on it, will perhaps fall into the same position as our railway company.
The minister's predecessor indicated his belief that competition could gradually be injected into international and domestic air services. I suggest to the minister that the restrictions imposed on the Canadian Pacific Air Lines have made it almost impossible for that carrier to continue operations. I suggest the time is now opportune for introducing a greater element of competition. This can be supported by statistics compiled by the government-owned air carrier, Trans-Canada Air Lines, which indicate that while it has shown a deficit largely attributable to the replacement of its air fleet, it was able to fly more air miles at a greater rate of occupancy than at any other time. I suggest that the future of aviation must be protected, and that this can be done by the introduction of a greater element of competition at this

stage by removing or relaxing those impositions placed upon the second major carrier in this country.
It is perhaps in the field of international aviation that we could hope for greater opportunity for the second major carrier because, of course, much of the traffic that they would be competing for would be drawn from United States carriers rather than in Canadian. Nevertheless, I believe that in Canada we can also provide C.P.A. with a number of runs and a greater opportunity to compete for both freight and domestic traffic at the same time.
I would like to say a little more on this subject, Mr. Chairman, but I realize it is currently under study. I hope that in the near future we shall learn the intentions of the government in this respect. As I said at the beginning, I hope he will also indicate that the department is doing everything within its power to encourage all aspects of aviation within Canada.

Mr. Chairman, may I express to you, sir, the congratulations of this group. We realize that in the future there may be conflicts. However, I am sure you will realize that those conflicts will not reflect upon our admiration and respect for you personally. We hope we shall not make your task any more difficult than that of your predecessor.
May I also express the thanks of this group to the minister for the extent to which he has attempted to bring to the floor of the house answers to the many questions we have asked over the last few months. We have appreciated the amount of detail and the accuracy of those answers and the spirit of co-operation we receive whenever we call on his good offices.
We recognize that this is one of the most important portfolios of the government. Across this nation there is a tremendous amount of questioning going on in the people's minds with respect to this whole area of transportation. We are searching for a pattern; we are searching for some direction as to where we should be going. We see the situation of two railroads competing with each other, one owned by the people of Canada and the other owned by private enterprise. Both are being subsidized, yet each is competing with the other. We want to know what will be the position of the small air line companies which have been formed in relation to T.C.A. as a government entity. We want to know where the trucking industry will fit in, especially when we have one of the railroad companies going into this form of transportation which is not receiving the subsidies that the railway transportation services are getting.
Supply-Transport
We want to know where the crown companies fit into this pattern. Unfortunately no one seems to be able to find out what this pattern is. We appeal to the minister to take this into consideration. Perhaps what we actually need is a full scale review of our transportation policy. Perhaps the minister could take a page out of the book of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Perhaps we should have a huge meeting like the resources for tomorrow conference and bring in not only the transportation people, the railway people and the air companies, but industry, representatives of agriculture and indeed some so-called "eggheads" from our universities. Let us have some economists, and perhaps even more important of all, let us have some sociologists, because more and more people in this nation are becoming more and more concerned about the fact that our population is beginning to concentrate in a few major centres, and what might be called the geographic and climatic focus is becoming even more pronounced as a result of this concentration of people within a small area.
I think we should bring in some university economists to decide just how much it is costing to put a great many people in a small area in terms of the goods and services which must be provided. What are we losing as a result of building traffic arteries in the cities so that people can drive their automobiles and spend hours of valuable time in them? Could we put that money into low cost housing? In other words, we need to make more serious value judgments in this whole area of transportation. I think the people of Canada would want leadership from the Minister of Transport in this very area.
I realize that we have a royal commission on transportation which is carrying on its work right now. We have already received the first volume of its report, but surely the minister will recognize that it is really a royal commission on railways; it is not really focused on transportation. Indeed, it is completely railway oriented. What they are suggesting is a transportation system, as it would appear to be necessary, so the railways could operate in what could reasonably be called a rational and intelligent way. But I think we should get a full scale review of transportation.
I understand there has not been such a conference since 1917. Well, let us have one now. Let us take maybe two, three years to allow industry and agriculture to prepare briefs, as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has done. Bring these people together. Give the conference lots of publicity and give the Canadian people some feeling that a pattern has been developed in transportation for this nation.

Supply-Transport
Over the last number of months we have seen in the newspapers signs of consternation -some among government supporters-over the situation which has developed within our railway system and within T.C.A. versus the smaller or, at least, the private air carriers. This is one of the problems we must solve. Also I feel that one of the difficulties about this royal commission on transportation is its suggested continuation of the very phases that I am rather concerned about. The Mac-Pherson report suggests that we need to cut down on the number of branch lines and our unprofitable passenger service; that we create a huge trunk line going across Canada, and possibly trucking will come into that trunk line. But still there is no clear indication of just how this is to be organized. I am wondering whether we are creating even more concentrations of people in metropolitan areas, and the smaller municipalities of Canada are going to be left more and more behind. I think this is not what the people of Canada want; I think this is not what sociologists, penologists and various experts in the field are seeking to bring about. What they are seeking to produce is the kind of society that will produce the greatest fulfilment for the people of this nation. We have to be very careful in our emphasis, and that is why I think there should be a full review of the whole transportation scheme to find a pattern. A conference would be a helpful thing at this particular time.
Since the estimates were last discussed on the floor of this house we have been quite happy to hear that the minister has announced that regional air carriers are going to be allowed to compete with T.C.A., especially in eastern Canada. Nordair and Quebecair will be able to set up transportation lines to smaller cities such as Oshawa and Kingston. The people of my riding are hopeful that Peterborough will be able to move into this area as well, because we are beginning to realize more and more that today industries need air service. Their executives must be able to move quickly from one part of this nation or this continent to another. It is a serious disadvantage for a smaller community not to have an airport which will handle at least smaller aircraft which those lesser companies -lesser in sense of size in comparison with T.C.A. and C.P.A.-will be using.
For that reason I hope the minister will make every attempt to encourage and give every bit of advice and help possible to those smaller cities that will be trying to improve their air services and their airports, runways and conveniences over the next number of months. I think this is a step in the right direction, because it will help to stop the concentration which we find is taking place in Canada and which I do not think is helpful,

even from the point of view of the Minister of National Defence in terms of the necessary needs of the foreseeable future.
Another matter about which I was a little concerned was the attitude taken by at least one member in the house with regard to some of the crown corporations which have been operating in Canada, especially in the north country. I refer particularly to Eldorado Aviation and the Northern Transportation Company. I am afraid these companies received a rather bad going over on one occasion during the debate in the house. I think it is foolish to look at either of these companies in the sense of their involving simply a transportation problem. Both these companies are inexplicably related to the uranium industry. The problem there, of course, is to service the uranium mines and to transport uranium at the cheapest cost to those who are buying it. This is what these companies are attempting to do.
I have been rather surprised at the line of argument that has been taken. These companies have been criticized because they do not seem to be making enough money, and T.C.A. has also been criticized because it is not making enough money, while on the other hand Polymer has been criticized because it has been making too much money. One really wonders what is meant by free enterprise, and the current definition would seem to be that it is enterprise for free by the people of Canada to be handed over free of charge to other entrepreneurs. I do not think this is a definition of free enterprise which a great many people would accept, certainly not in this department, and I am sure the minister will be very careful before any changes are made in relation to these crown companies which have provided such an admirable service to the uranium industry of the north country and have opened up a great many areas.
The final matter about which I should like to speak for a moment concerns my own constituency, and I am sure the minister will recognize what I have in mind. It is the problem of the Trent canal. We are very concerned about the suggestion that there may be some changes in the Trent canal system, because it is of such tremendous importance to the area I happen to represent. I should like to refer to a brief prepared by Mr. James P. McGrath, who worked on the Trent canal system for 34 years as canal superintendent for Peterborough county. I am not going to repeat the excellent summation of the importance of the Trent canal which was made by the hon. member for Simcoe East on the second or third day of the debate on item 1

of these estimates, but I should like to indicate just how important this canal system is.
It is important first as a reservoir to hold back water and thus prevent flood conditions developing throughout the entire valley. The maintenance of navigation levels in the canal itself is an extremely important matter. We have had a serious unemployment situation in this area, and we are hoping that over the next number of years we are going to be able to further develop the tourist industry, which has been unprecedented over the last quarter of a century. We are hoping that we will be able to carry out the views expressed by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and make the tourist industry not just the second major industry in our area but perhaps even the first. Navigation levels in the canal are absolutely imperative if we are going to attract the increasing number of people from the northern United States and southern Ontario who have become interested in boating.
In addition, of course, we have in operation on the Trent canal 27 power stations, some of which are privately owned. The Canadian General Electric Company, the Quaker Oats Company and other companies have such stations, and the availability of cheap power in the area is imperative if we are to maintain a growth economy and try to provide greater prosperity for these communities. I realize that there are some who feel that the changing of levels is a very serious problem in relation to the upper reservoir lakes; nevertheless I think the minister will appreciate that any serious change in the status quo will have a most deleterious effect upon a large number of people living in the lower areas.
I do not think any community wants to be one up on any other community. I do not think the system of providing air services by giving one route to one company and taking one away from somebody else and replacing that route with another is in our best interests. I think this juggling of air services that has been going on, especially on the west coast, shows a lack of foresight in a field which is probably the most important in a country as large as Canada, with its population as spread out as it is. That is why I come back to the point that there should be some kind of conference held or some kind of method devised to take a look from every direction at the whole field of transportation in 1961, 1962 or 1963, so we will know where we are going for the next 40 years. There should be such an examination at this time when there is such questioning, when there seems to be a crisis coming in the whole transportation situation and when we are at
Supply-Transport
the crossroads in so many areas, in relation to the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., in relation to private and public enterprise in air travel, with respect to where the trucking industry fits into the picture, and so on.
That is why when I refer to the Trent canal system I am not asking for any special privileges in this area. What we are asking for is an attempt to fit canal services into some pattern in relation to the other areas of transportation. I should like to read one statement by Mr. McGrath who, as I said, has had wide experience. He said:
Any deliberate man-made changes, such as the lowering of levels, might affect the navigable waters act and also the whole buoying system, rendering the navigation aids useless. The system could not be handled by groups as they could not possibly know the over-all picture.
He goes on to say what the results might be.
Since confederation the problem of transportation has always been foremost in the minds of Canadian statesmen, and I hope the minister will take into consideration some of the things I have suggested. They may involve wrenches and serious surgery in some areas of transportation, but I think we must come to grips with the matter and not be dissuaded by such slogans as free enterprise or private enterprise versus socialism, which are completely irrelevant to the situation in Canada today. What I think we need is a national policy. As it is one o'clock I will conclude my remarks.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate you on your appointment. I hope that in the days that lie ahead you will have the wisdom of a Solomon, and you have already shown that you possess such qualities.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the inadequacy of the methods employed in the Trent valley system, referring particularly to the opening and closing of the locks. Men are forced to open these locks by going round and round on a turnstile. This is very heavy work. I have known some of these men to take sick and be laid up for long periods as a result of the stress and strain involved in opening these locks. This waterway is being used more and more each year as the popularity of boating increases. I do not think it is fair to these employees to subject them to the drudgery of opening these locks in the same manner as they were opened over 40 years ago. As a matter of

Supp ly-Transp ort
fact, this system of opening the locks reminds me somewhat of the treadmills that were used in the early days of the first century.
I have a letter here from one of my constituents which I should like to read. He says this:
Sure, it is wonderful to go down to the United States where they have electrically operated locks and where the men have every facility to work with, and where they have a place where you can go round behind the lock at night if you are caught; but when a fellow has to walk around on the end of the treadmill like our lock keepers have to do, I don't know how you can expect them to be in uniform with a tie on. Over there, there is electricity at every lock; and from an economy standpoint, and for service to the public, every lock should be electrified, but I am afraid I will never see the day when they are.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this system has been neglected far too long, both from the standpoint of the people who are operating the locks and from the standpoint of the people who are operating the boats.
I wanted to make some reference as well to the low level bridges which are found on the Trent system. Surely it is about time, in this day and age, that we eliminated these places where boats have to stop in order that bridges may be turned. There is no place for such things in Canadian tourism today. Both the boats and the highway traffic are held up while these bridges are being turned.
One particular case is the low level bridge at the first narrows at Atherley. This is the place to which Champlain travelled over 300 years ago. Not only are the boats held up while the bridge is being turned, but motor traffic is held up as well. I have seen traffic held up there for a long period of time. This is a particularly important bridge. It is difficult to manipulate and the work is very hard on the employees. One would think we were still in the horse and buggy days when one sees such a system in operation. This condition is extremely annoying, in view of the fact the bridge forms part of the trans-Canada highway.
Let us get rid of these obstacles so we can invite boatmen from the United States, who are used to the electrification of locks in their canal systems, to come up here. The prospects are that many more boatmen from the United States will be using this water highway than have ever used it before. Let us do a good job so they will be proud to travel on our waterways and we will be proud to have them use these waterways.

Mr. Chairman, I shall deal only briefly with the first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport, but there is a matter that I feel strongly about and that
[Mr. Rynard.l
I shall submit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer). It has to do with the T.C.A. services in my riding.
The minister will agree that his department is already in possession of almost all the information required to look fully into the request submitted by the Kapuskasing chamber of commerce, which represents the town as well as the district of Kapuskasing with regard to the service provided by T.C.A.
From 1937 or 1938 to 1957, that district was served by T.C.A., first as part of a service between Toronto and Winnipeg, since Kapuskasing was located along the route between Toronto and Winnipeg. Later on, in 1945, that city was served by a direct flight from Toronto to Kapuskasing.
When the directors of Trans-Canada Air Lines decided to use Viscount aircraft, in October 1957, the service between Toronto and Kapuskasing was dropped.
I know that surveys were made by the Toronto office and that the department was led to believe that the cost of extending the runways to accommodate Viscounts would run extremely high.
However, engineers who are currently employed by the Spruce Falls Company, which operates a paper mill in Kapuskasing, and who must certainly know their business have made a thorough study of the situation. They claim that the estimate made by the Toronto office is much higher than the actual cost.
Mr. Chairman, it is an acknowledged fact that the construction of the Kapuskasing airport was a costly project since all buildings and facilities required for the operation of an airport, like a weather station, etc., were provided. Now, however, these buildings are almost left uncared for, except perhaps for what is needed by those who use what is commonly known as the private air service.
The airport is being used widely enough. As a matter of fact, I understand five or ten planes may be seen every day either landing or taking off. But that is not the important point. The important point is the service to which the population of the district has been used.
When the Kapuskasing airport was used by Trans-Canada Air Lines, it welcomed many distinguished visitors, for instance, Her Majesty the Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh during their visit in Canada in 1951; Her Majesty was then, of course, Princess Elizabeth.
In 1941, I think there was the visit of the late Duke of Kent, a few weeks only before his accidental death.

We had also the visit of Field Marshal Montgomery and of several other personalities. These historical events are proof enough that the Kapuskasing airport was a suitable airport and that it should have been maintained in good operating condition so that the service could be continued.
Our district is about 560 miles from Toronto and 600 miles from Montreal, maybe a little more. Moreover, our railway service is quite inadequate, and the need for a T.C.A. air service has become urgent.
If I chose not to mention this matter during the previous sessions, it is because I had promised the chamber of commerce officials that politics would not interfere with the efforts being made to induce the Department of Transport to restore the service we had enjoyed for some ten years. I did not mention the subject in the house, but I did keep in touch with the minister, and especially with his predecessor. I would not want to blame the present minister for what happened, but I would ask him to kindly reconsider the situation and to carefully look his files over concerning Kapuskasing airport. Then he will certainly realize how reasonable is the request we make in the name of people living in that outlying region where fast transportation is needed in case of emergency.
At the present time, for instance, to go to Toronto you have to ride on a bus from Kapuskasing to Cochrane in order to get a train connection, around 2.30 p.m. That train reaches Toronto around 8.30 the next morning. You have to admit that it is quite a long run, particularly when you consider that there is no sleeping car between Kapuskasing and North Bay. A serious study of that problem is a must and the request of the chamber of commerce should be considered so that the problem can be solved in keeping with the needs of the region.
The Spruce Falls Power and Paper Company of Kapuskasing provides the Canadian National with a yearly income of over $10 million, just for the shipping of paper and other materials that the mills require. So, it seems to me, considering all that, the department could have new surveys carried out and the situation studied, in order that an area which now numbers more than 35,000 is provided with a service like the one we are asking for, and which would fill a long felt need.

Furthermore, the minister will no doubt be interested to know that in the same district the Ontario hydro is carrying out at least two large developments and that, in addition, three other projects are on the way. Which means that for five to ten years an average of two or three thousand additional men will find work in the Kapuskasing and Cochrane districts, and they, of course, would find it most useful to have an adequate service for a population which should not be neglected any longer.
I hope the minister-I must say, by the way, that he found means to give his home town an airport, and I do not blame him for that-
It was not me but my predecessor.
