speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have just one other question in connection with the shipping policy and the amendment to the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement. From the statement made earlier by the minister it was not too clear that this would take some time. However, from what he said today it is now quite clear to me that it may be many months before it is implemented. The minister has probably seen the doubts thrown on the whole matter by a professor of Queen's University, I believe in Montreal. I refer to Professor H. J. Lawford. However, I do not intend to deal with that matter now. What I intend to deal with now is this. In the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of two or three days ago-I have just read it now and I have not it with me- there is to be found the statement that because of the amendment which will be made to the shipping policy and the extension of the restrictions on coastal trade, a British ship will now be able to move iron ore to an international port such as Cleveland, dump its load, go on to Duluth, take on grain and bring it down to a Canadian port either within the coastal limit referred to by the minister or outside it. I would like to know whether or not that is the case, because that is the affirmation in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. Is that correct?
Of course, this is an international voyage, and international voyages are not coastal voyages. The commonwealth merchant shipping agreement has nothing to do with international voyages.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank the minister for that answer. That was the understanding I had. However, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix goes on to say that this is going to create a great hardship to Canadian ports such as Fort William and Port Arthur in that the tendency will be to go to Duluth, get the grain and bring it to a Canadian port, since they cannot go to Canadian ports such as Fort William, Port Arthur, the lakehead ports, either within the restricted coastal area or below it.
If that affirmation is correct, it is going to restrict Canadian trade rather than help it; and I take it from the minister's answer that my statement is correct.

Actually the tendency will be, I am quite sure, for Canadian grain to be carried in Canadian vessels. As I said earlier, my hon. friend is talking about an international voyage. I do not think it will have the effect he mentions, because we have been

asked time and time again by Canadian shipping companies to take this action, and from the reaction we received from them I am quite sure they look forward to a substantial increase in the carriage of grain from the lakehead down to the lower St. Lawrence ports such as Montreal, Three Rivers, Quebec, Baie Comeau and Seven Islands.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue that point a little further. The minister says he has had a lot of requests from shipping interests. I should like the minister to produce the requests he has had from the farm organizations, because it is perfectly evident from what my hon. friend from Laurier said-and I must say I had not thought of it before he raised the point-that if the object of this restriction which the minister is proposing is to reserve the trade to Canadian vessels, it must be because the British vessels operate more cheaply.
What we may have in the future is a lower rate on grain from Duluth to Baie Comeau than we have from Fort William to Baie Comeau. That is going to be highly detrimental to the farmers of Canada and the ports at the lakehead, as the hon. member said.
I think the minister should reassure the committee immediately about what precaution the government intends to take to see that this does not happen.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend is placing this whole matter in very narrow perspective. He is dealing with all kinds of hypothetical effects of these regulations.
Let us not forget that these flags of convenience, for instance, have developed to the point where they have practically lost all national meaning. A great many Canadians are faced with unfair competition from people who have ceased to be truly British commonwealth citizens and corporations which have ceased to be truly British commonwealth corporations.
I just want to cite an example of how this matter has deteriorated. You may have a United States interest, for instance, which has a ship built in Holland, manned by a Greek crew, with Italian officers, and they register the ship in Bermuda and come and sail on the great lakes as a commonwealth ship.
I think there is unfair competition because of these flags of convenience. This situation was really becoming a danger to shipping and shipbuilding interests and I think it is absolutely proper that Canadian inland waters should be reserved for Canadian ships.
Practically all the trading nations in the world do this. When one studies the various
Supply

Transport
restrictions to protect national waters in all countries of the world one sees that the Canadian regulations are very far from being protectionist in the way my hon. friend suggests.

I was considering this from the point of view primarily of the wheat farmers. If we are going to have to pay a higher freight on wheat from Fort William to Baie Comeau or Montreal than the rate that is established by international competition from Duluth to Montreal or Baie Comeau, the minister is certainly going to hear about it everywhere from Winnipeg to the Rockies and into the Peace river bloc; he should make no mistake about it. If the minister is looking at this in terms of votes, there are far more voters in all that area than there are in the interests that he is talking about.
I am not saying anything one way or the other about the question of whether or not these waters should be reserved exclusively for Canadian ships. I do know that if we are going to sacrifice our market for wheat in the United Kingdom, or any large part of it, it is going to be too big a price to pay for this policy. However, it is a big question that will have to be debated when the matter comes before us in the proper way and I am not seeking to do it now.
It is not an academic question; it is the most practical question possible. If you ask any western farmer, the one reason for his enthusiasm for what my hon. friend for Laurier did in getting the St. Lawrence seaway built was that it would give us cheaper transportation for our wheat to the markets of the world and put us in a more competitive position. It was not that the cost of transportation would go up so that all that advantage would be lost. If the advantage is going to be lost and a competitive advantage is going to be given to the United States wheat growers, it will certainly be a sad day for us in this country. That is what this editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix seems to suggest, as the hon. member for Laurier so accurately pointed out.
Of course we would rather see Canadian carriers carry the wheat if they will carry it at the same price, and the minister ought to tell us what precautions the government is going to take to see that they keep their prices down to the same level as British carriers or foreign carriers from Duluth to Baie Comeau for carrying wheat. Otherwise we are going to have a storm on the prairies the like of which we have not seen for some time.

Ever since this policy was announced we have received absolutely no indication from any shipping company that

there was any intention of increasing these rates. What our shipping people were trying to get was the volume of shipping that was going to other shipping lines.
We have good ships here and we intend to build more. I think shipping companies, especially with the advantage they have at the present time with the subsidies and the closing of the inland waters, will be in a very good position to give excellent rates to shippers from the west.
Let us not forget that the shipping subsidy and the shipbuilding subsidy of 40 per cent is quite a great help to Canadian shipping on the great lakes and in the inland waters. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just briefly pursue one other matter connected with an answer the minister made earlier respecting Canadian ships operating under United Kingdom flag? The minister will remember that at one time there were close to 100 such ships operating under U.K. flag. However, I believe now there are only some 25. The minister indicated that in order to benefit or take advantage of the new shipping policy of the government those ships would have to re-transfer to the Canadian flag. I should like to ask what advantage there will be to those ships if they are transferred to the Canadian flag? My purpose in raising this question is that while there will be a subsidy of 40 per cent given to a Canadian shipbuilder this will not in any way assist the operation of the vessels. In other words, I am trying to say that the 40 per cent subsidy is only one step toward the equalization of costs among Canadian, U.K. and continental or European operators. Unless some enticement or assistance is given to that type of ship, what incentive now exists in the retransfer of those ships to the Canadian flag? What this all boils down to is, what assistance is being given under this policy to deep-sea operators?

Mr. Chairman, they may not want to come back under the Canadian flag, but if they intend to engage in coastal trade or trade on inland waters they must be under Canadian registry. As an example, I should perhaps refer to the Cloverdale of the Canadian Steamship Lines which was transferred to Bermudian registry. If the Clover-dale is to carry on with its work on the great lakes it will have to come back under Canadian registry.
As far as other ships at the present time under foreign registry and engaged in world trade are concerned, this new policy may not

be advantageous to them. Those ships have already been built, so there is no question of construction subsidy involved. I do not think it would be of advantage perhaps to those ships to come back to Canadian registry. However, there is a definite advantage for lakers and ships of that kind, engaged in coastal and inland waters trade, to come back to Canadian registry if they intend to carry on with that type of trade.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, are there any lakers which have transferred to outside registry? I was under the impression that all lakers, with the exception of the Cloverdale and perhaps one other, operated under Canadian registry. I am informed that there are quite a number of old United States lakers that have been placed under Nassau registry so they can carry on coastal and inland waters trade in Canada, and those ships will not be allowed to carry on with this type of trade if they do not register in Canada. If they do not carry a Canadian registry they will have to get out of coastal and inland waters trade.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There would be no advantage whatever to any laker that is presently under U.S. registry to change because the cost of operation is even higher there than in Canada.

The ships to which I have referred are old United States vessels purchased by individuals and placed under Bermudian registration, and are plying the great lakes at the present time with a commonwealth flag, engaging in trade from one Canadian port to another. These ships will not be allowed to continue to do that unless they come back to Canadian registry.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in regard to the payment of salvage subsidies. I suggest the minister should rectify this rotten act performed by that Liberal government. Mr. Chairman, I referred to a matter of pensions to 75 employees of the Canadian National Railways whose services are being terminated in the Niagara area because the C.N.R. is selling its franchise and equipment there. Mr. Chairman, I also asked several questions of the minister. While I have been away attending the meeting of the

I do have an answer in regard to the last question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester, which dealt with airport grants to the municipalities of Gloucester and Restigouche. The municipality must provide the land and agree to operate the field. The field must be technically satisfactory, and the departmental officials must make a traffic study in order to satisfy themselves that the traffic potential for local use exists. Once the officials have been satisfied in regard to these principles, the department makes a recommendation to the treasury board in respect of a federal grant to a maximum of $100,000 on a dollar-for-dollar cost-sharing basis. These projects in respect of both municipalities are now under study.

I understood the minister had made a statement in Dalhousie, New Brunswick, on May 12, in which he said the land had already been purchased and the airport would be built. This does not seem to be in accord with what he is saying now. He says it is under consideration. According to the reports in the press, he made the statement then that the land had been purchased and that the airport would be built.

It is easy to see that my hon. friend was not there when I made the statement. Of course, I did not expect him to be there at that time. What I said precisely was that the department had various systems of aid for municipally owned airports and that I met with the people in Dalhousie and explained to them that this type of airport required to be approved by the department. I also explained that if the municipality would buy the land we would meet every dollar that would be expended by the municipality on a dollar for dollar grants basis. Preliminary reports indicate that it is a very good location. Of course, they have not bought the land yet. Also, there has not been a complete survey from the Department of Transport relating to traffic possibilities and technical aspects of the location. I assure the people that if the municipality is ready to do its share for an airport we will do our part, and the department will share in the building of that airport dollar for dollar.

I accept the minister's statement now. According to his statement, I must agree with the minister that he had been misquoted.

Will the minister clarify the asssistance program for fishing vessels? Will this assistance be made available for new ships built to increase the fishing fleet, or only for new ships built to replace old fishing vessels?

I understand the interest of my hon. friend in these matters but, as I explained earlier, the regulations are being drafted at the present time. The section that deals with fishing vessels is being prepared by the Department of Fisheries. It will be part of the regulations which will be tabled as soon as they are passed by the governor in council. As I said earlier, I expect to be in a position to have these regulations ready for approval by the governor in council in a period of approximately two weeks.

May I follow up the question of my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo. The minister will recall that his statement was quite categorical on this point. His statement said that the assistance applied to vessels to replace existing fishing vessels. It did not say anything about a fisherman who had no vessel at all and wanted to build one. Is the minister now telling us that under this policy those vessels will also be considered?

Well, I do not want to add anything to the statement I made at that time. I do not remember exactly the wording of the statement, but I do not want to give misinformation to my hon. friend. I refer him to the statement I made on May 12. If any changes are made in the policy expressed in that statement they will be minor changes. I would ask my hon. friend to be patient for a couple of weeks and he will have the answer to his question.

As a matter of fact, we have been patient about this policy of the minister since last November. It now appears that the policy is not very much further advanced than it was last November. The minister rushed in here on May 12 and made a statement which was certainly blown up by his friends on Vancouver island into a $500 million program, about which the minister cannot tell us today whether a fisherman who does not own a vessel but would like to have one, can get any aid at all. The minister's statement was clear enough on that. In his statement on May 12 the minister said it was only to replace existing vessels. If anybody wanted to build a new vessel and did not have one already what would he do? The minister says that there are going to be minor changes. Surely it is a major change if

you are going to have the same assistance given to people who had not previously owned vessels. I do not know why the government would want to create a privileged class of those who already have draggers or trawlers as against other Canadians who surely have an equal right to consideration in this matter. Surely on a point as fundamental as this the government has made up its mind as one would expect of, to quote the Minister of Finance, any "normal" government.
Mr. Chairman, my only answer to the question of the hon. gentleman is to refer him to what I said on May 12. My statement stands as it was made at that time.
One further question. Are South African ships still regarded as commonwealth ships?

I do not know, South Africa may not be any more a maritime nation than Canada is. If there are any South African ships, how have they been treated since May 31?
We will deal with the problem when it arises. As of today, I am informed by the officials of the department that no South African ships are in the great lakes.
None?
Not so far as we know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the encompassing first item which covers a multitude of transport matters passes the committee, I should like to make a few observations about transport policy, particularly as that policy has affected in the past and in its ramifications in the future will affect Atlantic coast ports. I do this because earlier in the debate and, indeed, earlier today reference was made in discussion of the first item to the position of the Atlantic ports of Halifax and Saint John. To introduce what it is I wish to say I should like to quote from the earlier debate on item one on the 13th of May as found on page 4773 of Hansard. The hon. member for Port Arthur is reported as having said:
We know that there are now icebreakers and mechanical devices which can keep the port of Montreal open for almost the whole of the year. We also know that this is a delicate political problem because it is going to have its repercussions and its effects upon Halifax and Saint John. Yet I had a figure given to me by a man who is very prominent in shipping.
I would interject here that the hon. member did not give us any further information about this individual prominent in shipping, nor do we have his name. The hon. member went on to say:
He pointed out to me that the average saving per ton on freight coming through Halifax and Saint John in the winter as against that coming through Montreal is $12 a ton in favour of Montreal. One only has to look at the amount of freight coming through the two maritime ports in order to realize that we are in effect subsidizing the Atlantic ports by not pushing very strongly a policy to open up Montreal to winter shipping.
If I heard the hon. member right, earlier today on the discussion of this first item he advocated, in conjunction with the hon. member for Peterborough, a long look at a new transportation policy for Canada which would be based on cost. I am one of those who are perplexed by the advocates of socialism in the house who are everlastingly asking the government to become involved in a wider range of governmental activity and who suddenly become pure when it comes to a matter which affects promises given to regions of this country. My constituents would feel that I was remiss if I did not mention in the house on this first item a matter which is of
Supply-Transport
great importance at each year's sitting of the House of Commons to the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
I have brought into the chamber this afternoon a copy of the British Colonist, a newspaper published in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Thursday morning September 15, 1864. Hon. members will perhaps permit me one minute's recollection to establish why it seems to me to be important to quote this newspaper on this first item today. Why September 15, 1864? Well, this newspaper the British Colonist reports on its first two pages-members will be interested to know that this was a phonographic report-an account of a dinner given in honour of the delegates from Canada, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island by the delegates of the province of Nova Scotia, a dinner held in the Halifax hotel in connection with the conference on colonial union.
Hon. members will recall that it was the last evening in the month of August, 1864, that the Canadian government steamship, Queen Victoria, which some Prince Edward Islanders jocularly called the confederate cruiser, sailed into Charlottetown harbour. There was a group at the harbour that evening but history records that the islanders had not come to the harbour to see John A. Macdonald and the other delegates but to see the first circus in Prince Edward Island in 21 years. Indeed, there was a little trouble with lodgings in Charlottetown. John A. Macdonald never slept in Charlottetown. He slept on board ship in the harbour.
On Thursday, September 8, the delegates held a ball in Charlottetown and the following morning, when the meteorological and other fog had cleared away, they set sail from Charlottetown and went to Pictou, Nova Scotia.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The hon. member for Pictou applauds, as he fittingly should, for that charming community 100 miles from Halifax. There at Pictou some of the colonial delegates left the ship and went overland to Halifax. The others, John A. Macdonald included, remained on board the ship. The Minister of Transport might be interested to know that transportation in Nova Scotia in those days was in that high degree of refinement as a result of which the party that went overland arrived in Halifax after the ship which had circumnavigated half of the province.

On Saturday, September 10,	1864, the
colonial delegates met in the Halifax hotel. At ten o'clock in the morning the maritime delegates met and then, as now sometimes, could not agree among themselves. Within an hour the doors were opened and all the delegates from all the colonies resumed their plenary session. At 1.30 p.m. on Saturday, September 10, in Halifax the decision was taken to go to Quebec 30 days hence on the 10th of October. The following Monday, September 12, a great dinner celebrating the decision to proceed to the Quebec conference was held in the Halifax hotel. It is this newspaper which is the only extant report of what was said on that memorable night in Canadian history on which a great ball was held in the Halifax hotel celebrating the decision taken in that same hotel on the preceding Saturday that led to the Quebec conference and so to confederation.
These speeches are inherent in the heart of every resident of the maritime provinces. What was said that night is a part of the upbringing of every resident of our provinces. What was said? I quote from the newspaper itself which I have brought to the house. This great dinner was chaired by Sir Charles Tup-per, one of three illustrious Nova Scotians who have filled the chair of prime minister of Canada since confederation. Tupper introduced the speakers and Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, as he was to become, and then attorney general for Canada East, said among other things:
I have heard since I have been in Halifax the objection thrown out that there is much danger that you would be absorbed.
That is to say, by union or confederation.
It will be very easy for me to dispel such fears. I answer them by a question. Have you any objection to be absorbed by commerce? Halifax, through the intercolonial railroad, will be the recipient of trade which now benefits Portland, Boston and New York. If you are unwilling to do all in your power to bring to a satisfactory consummation this great question, you will force us to send all this trade which you ought to have through American channels.
I interject here that last year more than $400 million of Canadian imports and exports left Canada for foreign destinations or entered Canada from foreign lands via United States ports.
It is as evident as the sun shines at noon that when the intercolonial railway is built-and it must necessarily be built if confederation takes place-the consequence will be that between Halifax and Liverpool there will be steamers almost daily leaving and arriving at the former-in fact it will be a ferry between Halifax and Liverpool.

The phonographic report says that this was followed by cheers. We have not seen the ferry between Halifax and Liverpool as yet, but we would like to see it. Later in the same evening, the Hon. George Brown spoke in the Halifax hotel. The British Colonist reports him as having said, among other things:
But far in advance of all other advantages-
That is to say, of colonial union.
-would be this, that union of all the provinces would break down all trade barriers between us, and throw open at once to all a combined market of four millions of people. You in the east would send us your fish and your coal and your West India produce, while we would send you in return the flour and the grain and the meats you now buy in Boston and New York.
Then, Sir John A. Macdonald spoke, the father of confederation and Canada's first prime minister. This is what he said on that memorable evening:
I will not continue to detain you at this late period of the evening, but will merely say that we are desirous of a union with the maritime provinces on a fair and equitable basis; that we desire no advantage of any kind; that we believe the object in view will be as much in favour as against these maritime colonies-
Would the hon. member say from what document he is reading?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am quoting, as I earlier said, but evidently the hon. gentleman did not hear, from the British Colonist, a tri-weekly newspaper, published at Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Thursday, September 15, 1864. This edition records speeches made in celebration of the decision to advance to confederation. I was quoting from a speech made by Sir John Macdonald, and I continue:
In the case of a union, this railway must be a national work, and Canada will cheerfully contribute to the utmost extent in order to make that important link without which no political connection can be complete.
What will be the consequences to this city, prosperous as it is, from that communication? ... Build this road and Halifax will soon become one of the great emporiums of the world. All the great resources of the west will come over the immense railways of Canada to the bosom of your harbour.
Then, what did the Hon. Mr. Galt say on that evening in Halifax? He said:
If we are united we must have an intercolonial railway. I am an advocate of this great work, and it becomes an absolute necessity if a union of these provinces is to take place at all. . . But the railway is not to be looked upon as a question of cost, but as a bond of union, that will unite us in peace and in time of need.
Mr. Chairman, I cite these great utterances from our past, from a memorable night in the history of Canada, because these

speeches inhabit the minds and hearts of the people of the maritimes. When we hear, on the eve of the eruption of a new political party in Canada those who have espoused all sorts of government activity come into the house and say, stop all your activities when it comes to the maritimes, stop at the ports, then we say that purity ought to begin at some other place. The railway which linked us, without which there could have been no union and without us there could have been no union, was not built as an economic operation. It was built as a bond of union.
Lest any member of the committee think I am being partisan in my attitude, let me quote from a gentleman who did not adopt our philosophy. I refer to the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier who, on July 30, 1903, while prime minister, moved in this chamber for leave to introduce a bill to provide for the construction of a national transcontinental railway. Hon. members will find in Hansard of that date, column 7671, the following words attributed to him:
Let me observe that if we have used American ports, it is not because for five months in the year our own ports are icebound. Everybody knows that our ports in winter are just as open as the American harbours. Everybody knows, except Mr. Andrew Carnegie and the bulk of American public opinion, that if we have used American ports and the bonding privilege, it was not because our harbours were icebound in winter, but simply because we had no railways to reach them. In the face of this, are the Canadian parliament and people going to stand on their manhood and place us in such a position that at all times of the year, not only by one railway, but by two or more, we shall have access from January to December to our own harbours, and be able to say to our American neighbours:	"Take off your bonding
privilege whenever it suits you, we are commercially independent."
Well, that is what the leader of the Liberal party said, the only reason we were not making use of the ports on a twelve months' basis was that we did not have railway connections to them.
The Hon. W. S. Fielding, a distinguished Nova Scotian and later minister of finance, said, as reported at column 8557 of Hansard for August 12, 1903, during the same debate on the bill to provide for the construction of an international transcontinental railway:
With this road built, instead of being dependent on the Canadian Pacific Railway only, Saint John will have two strings to its bow.
Not a pound of traffic that goes to St. John now will be taken away, and St. John will stand its chance of getting a fair share of the new traffic to be created by this road. Halifax, with its peerless harbour, will have advantages which it has not hitherto enjoyed. Surely, sir, the time has come after years of deception, humbugging and trickery about the lines to the maritime prov-

inces, that faith should be kept with these people, and that they should have a through line running on Canadian territory from ocean to ocean.
It is interesting to note that in the preamble of chapter 71 of the acts of 1903 which followed that debate, the object of that national transcontinental railway is cited as being to secure the most direct and economical interchange of traffic between eastern Canada and the provinces west of the great lakes-and I stress this-and to develop commerce through Canadian ports.
Finally, I quote from the Statutes of Canada, 1955, chapter 29, section 21. In this act the term "national railways" is defined as a phrase which comprises the Canadian government railways, Canadian national railways and all the companies, not in Canada, mentioned or referred to in the first schedule of the act. Section 21 of that act which is on the statute books of Canada states:
The board of directors shall so direct, provide and procure that all freight destined for export by sea that is consigned within Canada for carriage to national railways either at point of origin or between that and the sea shall, unless it has been by its shippers specifically routed otherwise, be exported through Canadian seaports.
That is what we want on the east coast. We should like to say that one of the problems on which we in the maritimes are trying to formulate our thoughts and on which we feel we can usefully request federal action concerns the ports, particularly Halifax and Saint John. We have brought into the Canadian confederation two and more of the finest harbours in the world. These harbours are well served by inland and ocean transport lines. Our ports of Halifax and Saint John represent an investment of many millions of dollars on the part of the federal government and its agencies. That investment has been made and continues to increase in order to provide all of Canada with the outlet to the sea on her Atlantic coast which was promised us and which has been promised us through the years.
It is a well known fact that this investment at Halifax and Saint John lies virtually fallow during the season of navigation in the St. Lawrence river. The ports of Halifax and Saint John spring to life only when the winter ice has barred access to the inland waterway routes. It would be ideal to us if a way could be found to keep our waterfronts in Halifax and Saint John busy all year round. It is all the more important that these ports be utilized to the fullest extent possible during the short months in which they are Canada's only ice free outlets on the Atlantic ocean. Instead of this utilization, what have we found in the

Supply-Transport
past? We have found very substantial quantities of cargo imported and exported via United States ports, last year some $450 million worth.
The Minister of Transport will know that I have been in communication with him both by letter and verbally. I readily accept the proposition that the figure of $400 million is greatly distorted by one commodity, namely oil passing through a pipe line from Montreal to Portland, Maine. But even the remaining portion of this business would provide great employment for our people and a marked improvement in the Atlantic provinces' economy. Hundreds of millions of dollars in inland transportation charges and labour costs, and port service charges flow into the United States instead of staying in this country where they could contribute additionally to the prosperity of our people.
I venture the opinion that we in the Atlantic provinces are disturbed at this flow of Canada's foreign trade through other than our own ports. We are not chauvinistic in the maritime provinces. We were two of the original four in confederation. We do not insist that all import and export traffic be routed only through Canadian ports. We do not urge that all traffic move via our harbours. However, we feel that we can insist and urge that companies which derive their prosperity from the Canadian market and from national legislation should make a special effort to ship their import and export cargoes through our Canadian ports. We de not believe we can rely on such slogans as "Ship via Canadian Ports" alone. Every ship that enters or leaves a port in the Atlantic provinces means dollars and jobs for the people of these provinces.
In a recent study prepared by the port of New York authority it was estimated that that great port supported one out of every four of its 13 million people who live in the port area. We do not have similar statistics relating to Halifax and Saint John but, if we had them, no doubt they would not show any marked or significant difference.
Our ports now provide a multitude of jobs in a variety of fields. Men who are actively engaged in ocean, coastal and local water transport derive their livelihood in large part at the expense of our harbours. Thousands who perform services such as stevedoring, cargo checking, marine salvage, dock and waterfront terminal operations are completely dependent on our ports. Government employees such as those in customs, immigration, harbour maintenance and administration, and of most of the firms which supply goods and services to the vessels, all live on the prosperity of our ports. The combined earnings alone of the longshoremen and freight

handlers, watchers and checkers at Halifax and Saint John average $10 million annually. If we use the principle of free economic generation by which every dollar earned generates or creates at least $2 of additional income, we have nearly $30 million worth of income from these two ports.
We are therefore hopeful that, when port delegations representing the ports of Halifax and Saint John wait upon the Minister of Transport, as he has graciously agreed to allow them to do on June 26, there will be found a way to recapture part of the great volume of goods now passing in and out of Canada by other than our ports. This would be of assistance not only to the ports of Halifax and Saint John but to the entire economy of the Atlantic provinces and would keep faith with the pledges made to us throughout the years preceding and following confederation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It is not my intention to delay the passing of the first item, Mr. Chairman. However, the fact that the hon. member for Halifax found it possible to speak for nearly 30 minutes about the great politicians of the nineteenth century causes me to have less hesitation about asking a question of a politician of the twentieth century. My question is this. Will the minister inform me whether he has received from the chamber of commerce of Kapuskasing an invitation to visit Kapuskasing and the airport there? If so, can he say whether he expects to be able to find time to go there? I can assure him that he will be well received. Moreover, he can go there in safety with the planes of the Department of Transport. I can assure him that they will find it easy to land there.

I have received an invitation that I was obliged to turn down earlier in the year. However, I certainly look forward greatly to this visit to one of the most interesting parts of Canada. I shall be pleased to get together with my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, I did want to make some remarks as a result of the most amazing speech made by the hon. member for Halifax. I thought we were hearing the voice of Joseph Howe coming back to us again in this chamber; that is, Joseph Howe when he was leading the anti-confederates and before he came to his senses in 1870 and joined the federal cabinet. Evidently the hon. member for Halifax has not yet come to his senses in this regard.
The hon. member for Port Arthur did not in any way suggest that the port of Halifax should be abandoned. What the hon. member for Port Arthur suggested was that we need a complete transportation policy based upon

cost and service. I was sitting right next to the hon. member for Port Arthur, so I think I heard him accurately.
Service certainly means service to all Canadians, including those in Halifax. We are asking for a pattern which will allow a place for the port of Halifax, and surely the hon. member would not suggest that we are going to find such a place by holding back the clock, simply by spending money on transportation for coming to the port of Halifax at a cost of $12 a ton over the cost of going to another port. I would say this would be a disservice to Halifax and to all Canadians. If we carried this to its logical conclusion we would end all progress completely. This problem can be approached another way.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The supplementary estimate to vote 402 is vote 583.
583. Departmental administration, further amount required, $47,585.

I have one question to ask the minister with respect to this administrative item. The minister appoints individuals as agents of the Department of Transport, employees of other departments such as the Department of Public Works, who would be engaged in looking after wharves, docks, dredges and things of that sort. What arrangements are made between the minister's department and the other department? Does the Department of Transport stand responsible for any of the actions of its agents appointed in that way, in the performance of their duties?
If an agent is acting in the name of the Department of Transport we would be responsible.

When we were summoned to the other place, I was making a few comments on the remarks made by the hon. member for Halifax. I should like to take two or three moments of the committee's time to complete my remarks because I think they will be germane to this particular item. The committee will recall that the hon. member for Halifax made a gallant plea on behalf of his port. He is to be congratulated for this. However, in making his plea he completely misinterpreted the statement of the hon. member for Port Arthur and of myself. I would suggest this speech should have been made

Supply-Transport
certainly before the building of the St. Lawrence seaway and perhaps it should even have been made at the colonial office in the early 1800's before the St. Lawrence canal was begun. I am sure the hon. member for Halifax realizes that in 1961 no group in the nation can be served if it means holding back progress. The challenge of the 1960's is surely that of the government making sure that progress is not syonymous with economic injustice. What we in this corner want is a national transportation policy which will find a place for Halifax but a proper place for it.
I would ask the hon. member what he would do if, for example, technological development gave us the opportunity to keep the St. Lawrence open all year? Would he suggest that the government ignore it? Would he suggest that they hide it and thus bring about millions of dollars in additional costs for people bringing goods in through the port of Halifax? The hon. member rather sneeringly calls us socialists but in his plea for the survival of Halifax as a major port he gave the most eloquent explanation of socialism that I have heard since I arrived in this house. He called not upon the industrialists or merchants to send their goods through Halifax. He called upon the government to come in and redress the balance. Surely if the normal measuring stick of free enterprise, that of profit, is to be utilized, the hon. member is telling us virtually that by that yardstick goods would go through United States ports and certainly through the St. Lawrence seaway but he wants the government to come in and redress the balance. Evidently that is his idea of what free enterprise actually means.
What he is really saying is that there is no free enterprise and, of course, he is absolutely right. We live in a mixed economy based on subsidies. The coal miners of Cape Breton and the port of Halifax are subsidized. The wheat farmers are subsidized. We in eastern and central Ontario are subsidized by tariffs and so on. What we want is a planned approach which takes the whole business of subsidization out of this ad hoc unplanned political hocus-pocus which it is certainly in today. If it is costing us more to use the port of Halifax, the hon. member suggests that we should try to find some way to increase the cost.
This is the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaking. Has he not been talking to his minister during this current session, the minister who has been reading us lectures across the floor that we must cut down the cost of production, that we must lower our costs so as to make our goods competitive throughout the world?

Yet the hon. member suggests that we bring in goods through Halifax and increase the cost of production. This is certainly one of the most amazing contradictions within the bounds of a single department of government that I have heard during the present session. Surely it is exactly this sort of thing which is over-pricing our goods in the markets of the world.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has set up a productivity council to bring down the cost of production. Would the hon. member suggest that if, with regard to an industry to which the council turns its attention, the council decides there should only be 1,500 workers instead of 3,000 the nation should subsidize the other 1,500 workers? I do not think so. The minister is concerned about bringing down the cost of production. We are also concerned about bringing down the cost of production but let us plan it so that we can give some kind of economic justice to all.
The 1960's and the 1970's are going to bring about tremendous disruptions in the labour force. The Minister of Labour has suggested that we are going to have to have flexibility and mobility of labour such as we have never seen before. Yet the hon. member for Halifax, standing firmly on his free enterprise platform, tells us we have to try to keep the port of Halifax operating no matter what happens.
He never said any such thing.

The hon. member for Halifax used history or misused history to support his argument. When confederation came about there was one promise made and it will be found right in the British North America Act. That promise was to build the intercolonial railway and it has been fulfilled. We could no more promise to keep the port of Halifax operating at full volume than the people of Halifax or of the maritimes generally could guarantee the stage coach route from Toronto to Kingston. But we did do something. We did pledge that the people of the maritimes would never be put at a disadvantage. We did state that the well-being and prosperity of the maritimes would be guaranteed as a result of confederation. I leave it to the hon. member for Halifax to decide whether that pledge has been kept.

Item agreed to.
Marine services-
403. Marine services administration, including agencies, $1,032,610.

Mr. Chairman, I was not a member of the committee that examined the proposed amendments to the Canada

Shipping Act but I wonder whether those amendments contain any decision of the government with respect to a problem about which there has been a fair amount of argument back and forth over the last couple of years. I refer to the question of whether small boats, regardless of the amount of outboard power by which they may be propelled, should require a licence. I believe that up to now boats powered by outboard motors of less than ten horsepower have not required a licence from the department. Is that still the situation, and is it proposed to alter it in the amendments this session?
The limit is still ten horsepower but the amendments will give us authority to make regulations to cover all small boats.
At the present time the regulations would not permit a change by order in council without reference to parliament. Is that correct?

At the present time we could reduce it by order in council but what we intend to do under the new legislation is to extend the power of regulation and licensing to cover other types of boats such as sailboats and even non-powered vessels.

What about the minister's intentions with respect to licensing operators? I believe no licence is required at the present time irrespective of the age of the operator provided he is operating a small boat with a motor under ten horsepower.

We have arranged a conference with representatives of the provincial governments for September 6 and these matters will be discussed then. All these matters, including the questions of licensing operators, who will do the licensing, whether there will be a charge and so on, will be discussed at length with the representatives of the provincial governments.

I take it from what the minister has said that it is fairly obvious that it is his intention to make some rather radical changes both with regard to licensing of small powered boats and possibly operators as well. He referred to a conference on September 6 and the question of who was going to look after these matters. Are representatives of the tourist industry, tourist camp operators and so on, going to attend this conference?

We have a winter conference with representatives of the industry where they express their views and where there is every possibility for them to discuss all matters that might have a bearing on their trade.
Supply-Transport
The department has in mind very much, of course, the development of the tourist industry in Canada and there is no intention at the present time of bringing forward regulations that would more or less put the industry into a strait-jacket. We will discuss the matter with the provinces to ascertain who will issue licences, if licences are to be issued, and who will be responsible for the machinery because, so far as the Department of Transport is concerned we have doubts about the usefulness of setting up a huge machine to handle licensing of small boats. The matter has been discussed with the trade, and we are going to discuss it with the provinces. We will try to find the best formula to assure that there will be a minimum of accidents and problems. At the same time, we do not want to be so strict that we will restrict the trade.

I hope that if the new legislation is going to give wide open power to the cabinet, the minister will not make recommendations in the early stages, at least, that will be too radical in nature. I think the regulations should take into account the density of the traffic in various parts of Canada. Something that might be required in a heavily populated area where the area of the water is extremely small, would be quite different from what might be justifiable in areas such as northern Ontario where we have a great deal of water and a relatively small population. I would hope that bureaucracy would not run wild in connection with this proposal and start a program of empire building. We do not want to build up a big supervisory staff or to have new regulations that would be completely unnecessary in certain territories where traffic is very light and, perhaps in consequence, the accident rate is almost negligible.

That is precisely the point of view we had taken in our discussions with the trade last winter. We want to make it clear that the department has no intention of setting up a huge machine. We simply want to co-operate with the provincial governments and various bodies to try to avoid as many accidents as possible. We certainly do not want to set up a huge machine, and we do want to encourage the tourists as much as possible.

I would just urge the minister to go slowly, and sort of feel his way along in connection with these regulations. I think this is true also in the matter of any departure from the historic pattern in respect of the age barrier. I have lived in an area in which we have a lot of lakes, and 1 have observed that some youngsters can perform a very fine service for their

Supply-Transport
family, as well as contribute to their own amusement, if they are given by those in control of them modest power on their boats. A great number of them, irrespective of their rather tender age, operate small boats more efficiently than some elderly, inexperienced tourists who will come and rent a boat.
As I say, if these children are not given boats of idiotic power, they can perform a useful service for their families during the summer vacation by providing transportation back and forth, and so on. I would hope that some blanket regulation would not be developed under which no one under 12 years of age, or something of that kind, would be allowed to get a licence to operate an outboard motorboat of reasonable power. On the other hand, I must say that I see some very deplorable examples of bad judgment on the part of parents who allow young children to operate outboard motors of 18, 25 and even 50 horsepower. Having regard to the age of the youngsters, this is rather ridiculous. As I have said, however, I hope that the regulation will allow some discretion in this matter.

Item agreed to.
Aids to navigation-
404. Administration, operation and maintenance including fees for membership in the international organizations listed in the details of the estimates, $6,783,790.

I have just a few words to say about this item. I understand it relates to aids to navigation, which is a subject in which I have been interested for some years. I think for five years I urged the department to put markers on the Columbia river between the international boundary and Castlegar. Finally, they were placed there. It took a long time to get this accomplished, but it only took a couple of days' work by a couple of men to install them. These markers were very necessary, and there were some very narrow squeaks before they were installed involving United States tourists coming up in small craft who were unfamiliar with the channels.
I also have been urging that such markers be established on the Columbia between Arrowhead and Revelstoke. I am very glad to know that arrangements are being made to mark the river between Arrowhead and Revelstoke. I mention this at this time because of increasing water traffic from Portland in the United States north as far as Revelstoke on the Columbia river. Last year, there were about 100 craft involved.
Yesterday, I received a letter informing me there will be 10 to 15 craft going to Revelstoke this week end from points south of the border. There were a number of accidents last
year between Arrowhead and Revelstoke in which boats lost their propellers on sandbars. In these swift waters, shore markers are usually used and the people steer from one marker to another. I think in this instance it is a Department of Public Works official who acts as agent for the Department of Transport in this area. He has a lot of work to do, so this sort of thing has to take second place. In the meantime, we have these craft going up the river. The last trip made by one United States flotilla between Arrowhead and Revelstoke resulted in four boats losing their propellers and one suffered serious damage to the hull. There are no markers in this somewhat swiftly flowing stream to mark sandbars, logs and that sort of thing.
I suggest in view of the increasing importance of navigation on the Columbia, and because of the interest of more and more United States citizens who are finding out what a marvellous trip it is into the garden of Eden, it would be worth while for the department to have one of its officials in Vancouver make a visit to the district and examine the marking of the river between the international boundary and Castlegar, and between Arrowhead and Revelstoke. Then, as promptly as possible, he should see that these markers are set in place. We have had high water in that district lately, which tends to push these buoys out of place. They should be replaced as soon as the water starts to drop. I made the trip down the river with one captain and there were 11 buoys out of place for over six months. No one had been in there to replace these buoys which had been washed out by the high water. This is necessary in view of the narrow channels.
At any rate, we want to do all we can in the Kootenays to attract the United States tourists because they are coming up there and stopping over at our tourist resorts. They go into Kootenay lake and sometimes transfer their craft over to the Columbia or vice versa. We do urge the minister, therefore, to make certain that his department does all that is possible to make navigation safe. It is not an expensive job at all.
My final word is to suggest that the department should issue a rudimentary chart that could be sold to these people at the customs office at Trail when they come into Canada for use up the river. This chart could show where the markers are, and indicate what a red buoy, blue buoy or black buoy means, green lights, red lights and so on. More and more we are finding people without experience operating these boats in swift waters and in some cases dangerous waters. I make this plea at the request of the chambers of commerce in the district, the tourist resort operators and the local people generally.

I am informed that the director of marine works is going out to the Arrow lakes area later this month with the purpose in mind of trying to get a contract or contracts into operation in order to put up these markers. As far as charts are concerned, I think anything along that line would have to come after the markers were put into position. I do not know what can be done in that regard, particularly in the immediate future. However, knowing that part of the country quite well, knowing the hon. member's great interest in it and also his interest in the development of free enterprise of all kinds, I thought I should perhaps suggest to him that this would seem to me to present a great opportunity for him and some of his friends out there to institute a pilotage system in order to get these United States craft safely up and down this stretch of water.
I might inform the minister that we have instituted a pilotage system, but our pilotage system's main function is to direct these people to the proper stopping places in which many have an interest.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I observe that the Minister of National Defence has a roving commission tonight.
I have quit roving now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps he might help me with the matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport. It has to do with a dispute which has arisen between two entities over which the minister has jurisdiction. I refer to aids to navigation on the St. Lawrence seaway. The minister will probably recall that the Auditor General of Canada has, I believe, before some committee-whether or not it was the public accounts committee I cannot remember-made a recommendation that aids to navigation on the St. Lawrence seaway should be paid for by the St. Lawrence seaway authority and not by the Department of Transport. I should like to tell the minister that the recommendation of the Auditor General in that regard is totally unwarranted. I respect, of course, the opinion of the Auditor General, but I think I should inform the minister that the Auditor General did not possess the information which he should have had when he made this recommendation. Not only is the recommendation unwarranted but it is wholly erroneous and perhaps I may just take a moment or two in which to say why.
If the St. Lawrence seaway authority were to pay for the aids to navigation on the seaway, then why should not the authority pay for the pilotage or why should it not pay for a number of other matters that arise on the
Supply-Transport
St. Lawrence seaway? I should like to bring this matter to the attention of the minister for what it is worth and I believe it is worth something, although I doubt very much whether the government would take cognizance of anything I have to say. However, I bring the matter forward because I am convinced that it was settled a long time ago.
When these two entities, namely the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation started to negotiate on the question of matters that affected tolls, they immediately eliminated the aids to navigation and they said, "This is not a matter for us to determine or to consider; this is a matter for our respective governments". That was the situation in the United States and that was the situation in Canada. When the present government established the international tolls committee, it told the members of it, "here are the things upon which you must base your calculations in order to arrive at the amount of capital expenditure upon the seaway". That was done not under the previous administration but under this administration and I have no fault to find with this at all.
The only thing I want to bring to the attention of the minister is this. Aids to navigation on the seaway were not even considered. The matter did not go to the joint tolls committee because it was taken for granted that they would be looked after by the Department of Transport in the same manner that the Department of Transport looks after all aids to navigation east of Montreal and west of Montreal beyond the St. Lawrence seaway and in all other parts of Canada. I do not want to take an undue length of time in discussing the matter. However, I feel that the recommendation of the Auditor General was not only unfair but unwarranted and that the St. Lawrence seaway authority should not be charged with that item of cost as it was never the intention that it should be charged with it, either in the meetings that took place between the two entities or in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act which clearly sets out the powers and purposes of the legislation.

Not only do we listen with care to what my friend the hon. member for Laurier says but I might tell him that he has convinced me. I know that this matter was raised in the public accounts committee. My officials have explained the situation before the public accounts committee. We have referred the matter to treasury board and treasury board has told us to carry on looking

Supply-Transport
after the cost of these aids to navigation but to keep them in a separate account, and that is what we are doing.

Item agreed to.
Canals-
406. Administration, operation and maintenance, $2,398,550.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 406 carry?
Before vote 406 carries, may I ask whether the minister has had time since dinner to give consideration to the constructive suggestion I made to him about the Trent canal?
During the dinner recess I had a most interesting meeting with the truckers and I forgot completely about my hon. friend and his very good suggestion.
Does the minister say he has forgotten what my suggestion was?
For the moment only.

My suggestion was that the Trent canal should be given to Mr. Frost as a sort of consolation prize, in lieu of the $100 million that the Prime Minister has not given to him, although he promised it before the 1957 election, so that Mr. Frost could turn the Trent canal into a provincial park in the same way that the Quebec government would like to turn the Soulanges canal into a provincial park, and thereby relieve the federal treasury of its cost.
I am sure that if we were offering Mr. Frost 13 miles of a certain length of canal, he would not refuse just because he could not get 14 to one.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You do not know Premier Frost.

With regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, may I say that when he speaks of the Trent canal he is speaking of something that is very close to my home and also very close to my heart. The Trent canal starts at the lovely bay of Quinte in my riding. I am certainly not in accord with him when he suggests giving it away to anyone. I might inform him that it is one of the beauty spots of Canada. It is a real tourist attraction. While there may not be any direct revenue from it, it is a tourist attraction and indirectly that fact should make it worth while, more so now than ever before in the history of Canada. We have many more pleasure craft coming to our land and in our land. There are many more using the Trent canal than

there ever were in years gone by. I therefore cannot agree with this idea of giving away this canal that starts in my riding, which is such a lovely place. I would invite the hon. member to come up some time and I will show him one of the very special tourist attractions of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I must express a good deal of astonishment at the expression of the lack of confidence by the hon. member for Hastings South in the government of Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise the matter of grants paid in lieu of taxes to my municipality of Thorold by the St. Lawrence seaway authority in respect to the Welland canal and Welland canal lands. The St. Lawrence seaway authority took over the operations of the Welland canal on April 1, 1959, and prior to that date the canal municipalities received yearly grants in lieu of taxes from the Department of Finance under the Municipal Grants Act.
My town has an area of 1,390 acres. Of this area, the canal owns 483 acres, 87 of which are leased. The canal actually makes use of 396 acres, nearly 30 per cent of the area of the municipality, and this is over 65 per cent of the taxable area of the town.
The Department of Finance paid grants in lieu of taxes in respect to certain canal buildings. These buildings were greatly depreciated, much more than similar buildings in town, and they had an assessment of around $170,000. The Department of Finance then paid something around 10 per cent of the toted taxes of the town until March 31, 1959. For the rest of 1959 and since-that is, for the other nine months of 1959 and since-the St. Lawrence seaway authority has refused to pay any taxes in respect to buildings, and this reduces their taxes down to something around 8 per cent of the total taxes.
It may be argued by the St. Lawrence seaway authority that the town gives no services in return for these grants, but I have seen our police out in force protecting their buildings and I have seen our firemen fighting fires in canal buildings.
I attended a meeting in St. Catharines last year between the municipalities and officials of the St. Lawrence seaway. Mr. Rankin, the chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, was there. He received us very well. One statement which he made was that grants would be arrived at on a different basis, but the amount that the municipalities would receive would vary very little from what they had received in the past.
I suggested to him at that time that this was the thin edge of the wedge in getting out of

paying a certain amount of taxes, and he said this was not the case. The point is that ever since the town has not received any grants in lieu of taxes in respect to buildings, and this amounts to about $10,000 a year or 2J mills.
Since I have been in parliament I have heard two ministers of finance state that crown corporations would pay grants in lieu of taxes on a fair and equitable basis. I understand that in the United Kingdom the government pays grants in lieu of taxes in respect of all crown properties and buildings.
The St. Lawrence seaway authority states that they are not bound by any assessment act, municipal act or the Municipal Grants Act, all of which is probably true. But I do suggest that no matter on what basis grants are paid, the decision is made on a unilateral basis and we would like to know what that basis is.
The amount of $10,000 is considerable for a small municipality, particularly a municipality that has provided services across tax free land of the canal for well over 100 years, as well as providing free services to the canal all this time.
When I was presenting the case of the municipalities here in 1952 I referred to the fact that I had seen an old picture of a hand fire fighting brigade fighting a fire in some canal structures. This picture was 100 years old. In 1951, for instance, our fire brigade fought 22 fires on canal property. I realize there is some history back of all this in connection with the Welland canal and the old Welland canal rehabilitation about which the St. Lawrence seaway authority would not be aware.
The present canal cuts across our natural drainage system and in 1949, as mayor of the town, I applied to the Department of Transport to have the effluent from a sewage disposal plant go into our natural drainage system running along the canal. The department objected at that time to this proposal and offered to pay $100,000 toward the cost of an interceptor sanitary sewer.
At the time of the rehabilitation of the old canal an arrangement was made that the department would forgo contributing this $100,000 and would go ahead and carry out more rehabilitation, which was done. However, at the same time we have been denied the right to build a sewage treatment plant along our natural drainage outlet and will be forced to pay the cost of piping our sewage through an interceptor sewer a distance of eight miles or more.
The town of Thorold in my constituency very reluctantly accepted this arrangement with the department, but they did so thinking that they would from then on be able to
Supply-Transport
draw a grant in lieu of taxes in respect to canal properties. Now these are being considerably reduced and I think it is very unfair. The other canal municipalities are not similarly situated. Thorold is on the brow of a mountain; it contains all the flight locks, and at that particular point there is a concentration of buildings. This condition does not obtain to the same degree in the other municipalities.
Other municipalities are of course affected by the canal because they have duplication of services. Some of these municipalities must maintain firefighting equipment on each side of the canal; they must have two sewage plants, which they would not need if the canal were not there.
I would like to hear from the minister on what basis grants in lieu of taxes should be paid by the St. Lawrence seaway authority. I would like to know whether or not the Department of Finance was wrong in paying the grants previously on buildings; and if they were wrong at that time, why were they paid? I should like to know on what authority these grants are paid, and why they are not being paid now in respect to buildings. As I have said before, we do give protection to their buildings.
One other matter I should like to refer to, has reference to the interruption of street traffic in the city of Welland caused by boat traffic in the canal. The canal goes through the city. There are no locks nearby and for some miles both north and south of the city the canal is a straight sailing level. The boats necessarily traverse the canal at reduced speeds and when they bunch up in groups of three or four some hundreds of yards apart in traversing this area the bridges are sometimes up for 30 minutes or more at a time. This presents a real street traffic problem and affects the economy of the city.
I should like to ask the minister whether he can intercede with the St. Lawrence seaway authority in an effort to see that the boats do not bunch up in this way. I am sure that if the minister was successful in such an attempt his efforts would be very greatly appreciated. I would also like the minister to reply to my question in respect of the reason why the department is not now paying grants in lieu of taxes on buildings.

Mr. Chairman, if you will permit me I should like to say in regard to the two items referred to by the hon. member for Welland that I should be pleased to provide an answer. However, I point out to the hon. member that these two matters are strictly within the jurisdiction of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. I shall accept the two questions as notice and attempt to provide an

Supply-Transport
answer when we reach our consideration of the estimates on the St. Lawrence seaway.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the minister could give some consideration to the supplying of uniforms for the workers on canals, including the operators, lockmen and those individuals who work on the walls. I have particular reference to the canal at Sault Ste. Marie where, on the United States side, the employees are all supplied with uniforms while on our side they are provided only with caps, and perhaps shirts. I think there would be a great deal of improvement in the general appearance around these canals and locks were the employees dressed in uniforms.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that is a very good suggestion. The treasury board has ruled that, for the time being, our canal employees will be supplied with caps only, because it would be very costly to provide complete uniforms, particularly in view of the fact that many of them are on rough work, and work with greasy machinery, and would require more than one uniform per man. It has been decided, therefore, at least for the time being, to supply caps only, but I should not like the hon. member to feel that the door has been closed on his suggestion.
