Mr. Chairman, I could not allow item 406 pertaining to canals to be carried without saying a few words on a matter of concern to all members. I refer, of course, to the Soulanges canal.
As everybody knows, the province of Quebec conceived a splendid plan to use and develop this canal for another purpose, not only for the benefit of this particular area, but of the whole province.
I should like at this stage to recall briefly that the federal government had once expressed its readiness to sell all the canal property to the Quebec government for the nominal amount of $1. Subsequently the present government was willing to sell to the province of Quebec an area of about 13 miles, reserving however that one-mile stretch that the Quebec government considers most important for its proposed development, namely the Cascades area.
The most surprising point during that discussion was the letter sent to the newspapers under the signature of the hon. member for Vandreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais). Indeed, I mentioned it during the examination of item 1 of the Department of Transport's estimates. In that letter, the hon. member stated that he alone is against this transfer of land to the province of Quebec. Moreover, the hon. member stated that he was to be

held fully responsible for the action he has taken.
Now, it seems that further negotiations were carried out between the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec. The item under consideration gives us an opportunity of presenting our arguments in connection with that matter.
Knowing as I do how highly interested the minister is in this matter, I am sure he would have been most disappointed if we had not mentioned that subject, because he will now have an opportunity not only of making his point but also of informing us of all the discussions which may have been going on recently. Moreover, the minister will be able to tell us what happened after the newspapers announced the government's offer to sell that part of the canal which is called Les Cascades.
I would therefore ask the minister to state his arguments in connection with this question. I am sure he will be grateful to me for having made it possible for him to do so and I may have a few questions to ask him afterwards.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words concerning the subject on which the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) has called the minister's attention.
I am not satisfied with the reply the minister gave me this afternoon, and rightly so, because if he remembers well, when I asked him certain questions concerning the Soulanges canal, he told me that all the chambers of commerce of that district had asked him to keep the mile-long section of canal in the neighbourhood of Point des Cascades. I then asked him to name those chambers of commerce but he did not do that; instead, he merely produced this advertisement which was prepared jointly by the Soulanges chamber of commerce, the people who work on the Soulanges canal and others. However, that advertisement did not mention any representations by chambers of commerce. I have here all the representations made by the chambers of commerce, and they all asked the minister to make the transfer at no cost to the government of the province of Quebec, of all the Soulanges canal properties, not with the exception of a one-mile area, but of all the properties, to make possible the carrying out of all the projects that were mentioned, thus giving the people of Soulanges county a source of income which would enable them to prosper as they did before the canal was closed down.
It is therefore obvious that all the chambers of commerce were in favour of the transfer to the province of Quebec of all the proper-

ties, for the purpose which the minister knows.
In my opinion the minister should admit that he had no resolution from the citizens of Soulanges except the pamphlet I mentioned.
The minister should also tell us how long he intends to have that advertisement carried before deciding whether or not he will give to the province of Quebec the mile-long section of property he is retaining at present. In my opinion, the house is entitled to know whether the offer will last for a month, six months or a year. The longer this matter is delayed, the more difficult it will be for the government of the province of Quebec to undertake its program.
I do not wish to make any personal remark but the minister doubtless remembers the statement he made during a political meeting held in the county. I understand he said later on that he regretted having made that statement but there is no doubt in the minds of hon. members that it is the member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges who is delaying the transfer.
After all, if this could be really beneficial to the industrialization of the area-and 1 hope so because it would be in the best interests of the people-it seems logical that such industrialization should take place on the upper side of the canal, in the neighbourhood of Coteau where there are already two railways, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, while on the Cascades side there is no railway at all. There is an excellent road but in addition to a road, in order to promote the industrial development of the area, other means of transportation are required, therefore, I suggest that the ideal location for industrial development is the upper part of the canal.
I should like to ask the minister whether he got a resolution from the chambers of commerce and, if so, whether he would table it now.

The hon. member for Laurier is asking for the tabling of certain documents from the Soulanges chamber of commerce, I must tell him that he knows nothing about the matter, because a few days ago he mentioned there were eight chambers of commerce in Vaudreuil-Soulanges, when actually there are only four; one for the Soulanges area, one for Rigaud, one in Dorion and another on Perrot island. Only two cham-
Supply-Transport
bers of commerce have submitted resolutions, asking us to transfer the entire Soulanges canal to the province of Quebec for the purpose of setting up a fish-breeding station and a bird sanctuary. And those chambers of commerce were influenced by a small group of politicians in that county who wanted to create obstruction and delay the solution of the Soulanges canal problem.
Hear, hear.

When the hon. member speaks of industrializing the upper county, the Coteau du Lac district, he just wants to create confusion and misunderstanding, because we have no sites there. If there is to be industrialization there, it should be the sole concern of the people in that community, of the chambers of commerce. It is up to them to promote any industrial development.
Since 1956, the Soulanges chamber of commerce took some steps jointly with the industrial expansion committee and the Soulanges canal employees, and even spent a lot of money on publicity, to attract industries in the Soulanges canal area, no matter where.
The only site belonging to the Department of Transport which may serve industrial ends along the Soulanges canal, is at Cascades Point, about two miles from the seaway.
It is true that there is no means of communication by rail. But at Coteau landing or Coteau station, those properties that are mentioned do not belong to us.
The people of those localities should start something themselves to bring industry into the district. And if the friends of the hon. member for Laurier in Quebec decided to build the roads that were already started in 1959 and 1960, the district would know what it is to be industrialized.
A follower of Mr. Lesage.

Mr. Chairman, when we offered the province of Quebec 13 miles of the Soulanges canal for camping sites and fish hatcheries which would delight fishermen and so on, the Quebec department of fisheries and game would have immediately accepted our offer if they had been in earnest.
They refused it for one reason only, the fact that those people, like the hon. member for Laurier, often talk through their hat. They made promise after promise. They promised to erect buildings on the premises, that all the fishermen in the province of

Supply-Transport
Quebec would gather there and fish all kinds of fish-perhaps cod, I do not know-but they forgot one thing, namely that the present roads and bridges of Dorion, St. Ann and Perrot island, which were adequate for the people of Montreal island who often go fishing and holidaying in the Soulanges area, are not adequate for present-day traffic. New bridges had been started in 1960, but the Quebec Liberal government has stopped the work. The department of fisheries and game is more concerned with developing parks and fish hatcheries than the provincial government is concerned with solving a major traffic problem at the mouth of the county. That is the reason why the Quebec government has refused our offer. It is an excuse for not fulfilling another fantastic promise they made.
If no reasonable offers are made for the purchase of that part of the canal which we have put on sale, or if they do not involve enough employment opportunities, we will turn over the whole canal to the province of Quebec, and we will see whether the Lesage government was in earnest; we will see whether they can carry out their plans for a fish hatchery and a bird sanctuary.
The famous member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) has been trying to defend the position of the Liberal government of the province of Quebec. But why? He knows nothing of the interests of the people of Soulanges. The only thing we are trying to do is to diversity the economy of the constituency of Soulanges. This is none of their business. They have all the problems they need in Montreal, so let them deal with their own problems before sticking their noses into things they know nothing about.
A diversified economy is a must for Soulanges; to develop Soulanges into a centre for tourists, fishermen and bird lovers will not improve economic conditions, nor will it help the citizens of Soulanges. It may help a few of the friends of the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont and of the hon. member for St. Ann who would very much like to go fishing there, but it will not settle the problems of the people I represent.
Anyhow their argument does not hold water as we offered more than 90 per cent of the canal property for purposes now approved by the provincial government. We only want to keep 10 per cent of that land in case some industries would want to estab-
[Mr. Bourbonnais.l
lish themselves immediately or within a few years' time, so as to create employment for the residents of the Vaudreuil-Soulanges county.
This country has not only sportsmen but also farmers and workmen who have to leave their home to earn a living elsewhere. If employment could thus be created at home, our people would not need to go away and earn their living in Montreal.
Unfortunately members like the hon. member for Laurier, do not understand those problems; all they want is to confuse the issue.
You do not know anything about the province of Quebec.

He makes much of some resolutions which he has received from municipal councils, but you will have noticed that those resolutions are always in the same style and are all from the same source. He will not go because he is afraid. He is a stranger in Quebec. He was admitted out of charity.

Mr. Chairman, the member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont asked me first of all to clear up this matter of the Soulanges canal. Well, I believe I granted his wish this afternoon. Unfortunately, I think he was absent from the house when I explained the situation as far as my department is concerned.
I am asked for how long this offer of land for industrial purposes at Cascades will stand. The offer is for a period of one month and it is already a week since this offer was advertised in Canadian papers. In addition, our trade commissioners throughout the world have been informed. I should also like to inform the hon. member for Laurier that we have already received a couple of offers which we are now considering.
I feel that the stand taken by the federal government is both logical and consistent, moreover it is justifiable. Indeed, I sincerely

think the people of Vaudreuil-Soulanges will come to realize that the government has acted in their best interest.
I know it is nice to have a place where people can fish and relax, but there are many other places like that in Quebec. A great number of the lakes which are available to the public-
There are the Laurentians.

-probably offer advantages which are greater than those of Point des Cascades. At any rate, we did not want to make any trouble. We were willing to do our share. That is why we were ready to give not only thirteen miles of canal but even the canal bed; we were even willing to give properties, buildings, and even a mill. I sincerely feel that with those thirteen miles of property along the canal, the provincial government could have made a very fine park and set up a whole series of scientific stations where the fish habits could have been studied and where all kinds of fish-breeding experiments could have been carried out.
On the one hand, they seemed to insist on having also Point des Cascades, which is indeed a wonderful and large enough location. But on the other hand, many people-I am not saying everybody, I am not denying that municipal corporations passed resolutions asking that everything be handed over to the provincial government-have made representations to the government and, as my hon. friend from Vaudreuil-Soulanges was saying earlier, two or three public bodies have, for some years, been attempting to promote industrial development at Point des Cascades.
All we want is one month, in order to have a chance to advertise the location and see if any industry would be interested to build a plant there. Let us not forget that while parks are fine it is better to try to get industries in a rural place like this which was deeply affected by the closing of the Soulanges canal and the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.
To date we have received two offers from industries and they are being considered.
But as I was saying a moment ago, the problem of the industrial development of Point des Cascades will be under consideration for a month. And, if after a month we should find that offers made were not too attractive

and could not provide enough employment, we shall be delighted to transfer the whole canal to Quebec.

There is no doubt about
it. Besides, if there was ever a government that proved it, ours did. We are trying by every possible means to urge industry and private enterprise to create job opportunities for Canadian citizens. The Minister of Transport, who lives in Three Rivers and not in my constituency, of course does not understand as well as I do the problems that exist in my area. The Minister of Transport was agreeable to surrendering the whole of the Soulanges canal as was part of the population in my county. It is as simple, as clear and as honest as that. I know what problems they have. Members opposite think it extraordinary for a minister and a member of parliament even if they do not always see eye to eye to finally come to terms. Well, what prompts them to rise is the unity they can see in our party compared to theirs. I ask them to turn to the Lesage cabinet and see what is going on in there.

Mr. Chairman, I would very much like the minister to answer the question I put to him earlier. What happened that made the government change its attitude after having accepted the original offer from the province of Quebec?
My second question is this. When there is an agreement between the province of Quebec and the federal government, to implement a project which is consistent with public interest, since when must the government yield before a member who is opposed to the project and states he is the only one to object?
He is a good and honest member.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont would like to know what made me change my mind. First, let us recall certain facts during the discussions with the province of Quebec. The province wanted to buy for the nominal price of $1 the whole property of the Soulanges canal to create a fish breeding station there.

I agreed to meet them. On that occasion, my first words were to express my amazement that they wanted all the canal properties for $1, and that they refused to consider any other proposal. I told them that personally, I had no objection to their request but that I found them hard to please. Afterwards, I heard the arguments of my hon. friend for Vaudreuil-Soulanges which seemed most reasonable. I should like to take a few moments of the time of the committee to discuss this item. On the face of it, it appears to be an item for $8,200. However, in reality, to the citizens involved, it represents an item more like $6.2 million. Now, one does not have to be an accountant or belong to the Glassco royal commission to understand that statement.
In the first place, this vote makes provision for an increase from $20 to $30 per month in the amount paid by the government to retired railway workers in the maritime provinces and throughout Canada. At the present time there are approximately 4,000 people relying entirely for their income upon these cheques issued by the provident fund. These people live in the maritimes predominantly, but some of them are located in various parts of the country as a result of being transferred while employed by the government railway. The figure I mentioned of $6.2 million is an accurate figure according to reports I have received.
The provident fund is maintained at the present time by deductions at source from all concerned of 1.5 per cent of the salary of approximately 2,000 men employed by the Canadian National Railways. The fund also receives a grant, by statute, of $100,000 from the Canadian National, together with the deficit required which the Canadian National must pay to maintain this fund. Last year the deficit of the provident fund exceeded $6 million. I understand that since 1922, when the Canadian National took over the administration of this fund, the total deficit met by the Canadian National has exceeded $75 million.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, it seems obvious that if the Canadian National, because of its inheritance, has paid the provident fund $75 million since 1922, then it is fair to state that the Canadian National has contributed its share. However, I question

whether the government of Canada has contributed its fair share to these railway workers. In 1940, there were 10,000 people in receipt of benefits from this fund or still contributing to the fund. The last figures I have, for 1959 indicated that this figure is now less than 6,000, made up of approximately 2,000 contributors and 4,000 pensioners.
I believe that the time has come for the government to take another look at this matter. Financially, it does not make very much difference, as long as the Canadian National takes care of the deficit because, although it appears that the government of Canada contributes only $8,200, when the government picks up the Canadian National deficit, it means in actual fact that the government is paying $6 million or $7 million annually. As I said a moment ago, I think the time has come for the government to take a very close look at the Intercolonial Railway provident fund. At the present time the people administering the fund are located in Moncton, New Brunswick, and they are entirely Canadian National employees. I suggest that the minister should consider the possibility of transferring the administration of the provident fund under his jurisdiction. Notwithstanding the fact that these employees worked for Canadian National, the pension cheques they receive have "Department of Transport" printed on them, and they are government of Canada cheques. If the government is carrying the load, then the government may as well get the credit for the full amount it pays rather than for the amount of this item.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I suggest also that the statutory increase in the pension payment from $20 to $30 is not sufficient. The amount of $30 was authorized many years ago, and today it is away out of line. There are very few people involved who are in receipt of this minimum pension. All of them gave many, many years of service at a time when railway wages were very low.
The act incorporating the fund was passed in this house in 1907, and it defined employees as employees of Her Majesty. The people for whom I have been speaking, many of whom I represent, are very disappointed over the fact that, notwithstanding an act of parliament which says they are employees of Her Majesty, they were not included in the assistance rendered by the Minister of Finance in 1958 when this house authorized increases in the pensions of retired members of the armed forces, the R.C.M.P. and the civil service. I should like to quote from the Financial Post of June 3, in connection with this matter. The article is entitled, "Sealed Tender System Urged by Air Transport Companies" and it reads as follows:
The Canadian aviation industry has asked the government to call for sealed tenders on future air transport contracts.
They should be opened in the presence of other bidders, the airmen argue.
This was one of the resolutions passed at recent meeting in Victoria of the Air Industries and Transport Association.
The airmen were actually complaining about Autair Helicopter Services, the controversial Montreal-based company which has been in and out of the political headlines since its formation.
It was claimed that last year Autair was granted a contract to supply helicopter services in the Arctic after it had been given a second chance to bid.
That statement does not come from me. I did make a similar statement in the house some time ago. The minister said it was not true. Here the Air Industries and Transport Association are taking this matter up and saying the same thing. Why are they doing that? They are doing it because they know full well that the company was allowed to submit another tariff after another company had entered into negotiations with the department. Then the article goes on to say this:
The association has also asked Ottawa not to give contracts to operators who have to lease special equipment from the U.S. if a Canadian operator already has such equipment on hand.
Autair was again the target, as it leased a large helicopter from the U.S. to handle part of the Arctic contract.
Again I put on the order paper questions having to do with this matter and very little information has been obtained from the minister. Here is the resolution which was passed by the Air Industries and Transport Association. I shall just read the governing clause which is as follows:
Now, therefore he it resolved, that all government contracts for air transport be requested on a sealed tender basis with a definite closing date and time and that such tenders be opened in the presence of any bidders desiring to attend and also a representative from the air transport board to advise on interpretation of licensing and tariffs.
This is the company which received from the government last year $183,500 for a contract which it had from the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys for the continental shelf project and for topographical work. This was for work done in 1960. The amount of the contract was $183,500. I presume that by now the company has been paid this amount. This amount was paid notwithstanding the charge that was made in the House of Commons that they were not the lowest tenderer.
From the evidence that was adduced at that time it was clearly indicated that again they had been given a second chance to tender. This is the company that also operated in the province of Quebec under the old regime of the late Mr. Duplessis without a licence from the air transport board under the Aeronautics Act. There is no doubt-and I put this on record previously-that when Autair Helicopter Services applied to the air transport board for a licence it was turned down; the air transport board declined the application. However, on appeal being made to the minister, the minister allowed the appeal.
This contract has been given to a company which, notwithstanding all sorts of protestations, has had its insurance cancelled twice and, has had no less than eight accidents; indeed it has had more than that number. I should like to put on record, Mr. Chairman, and I now ask permission to table the record of accidents of Autair Helicopter Services on the continental polar shelf contract. They had eight accidents during the years 1959 and 1960. This information is obtained from sessional paper No. 211B tabled in this house on May 16, 1961. I should like permission to table this list of accidents.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not too sure as to the intention of the hon. member. He has mentioned that he wanted to table the document.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What I mean is that I want to have it printed in Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee agree that this document be printed in Hansard at this point in the remarks of the hon. member?
Agreed.
I have no objection. However, Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind you that this document has already been tabled in the house. It is an answer to a question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is already tabled.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; it has not been tabled in the house. It has been made an order for return and therefore it is not on Hansard. 1 think I am entitled to make a copy of the order for return and to put it on Hansard in order to indicate the number of accidents this company has had in the last two years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I understand the question of the hon. member, he wants this to be made part of his speech instead of reading it. I think that is the request the hon. member is making.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we want to be careful about the precedents that we establish. I understand

this is a document which is already in the possession of the House of Commons. The hon. member wishes it to be recorded in Hansard without reading it. It seems to me that if we adopted this as a practice we would have Hansard filled up with quite a number of documents already in the hands of hon. members. Would it not be better if the hon. member drew our attention to the source of the information and simply summarized the accidents about which he has this information?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman; I intend to put it on Hansard myself if I am not saved the time of doing so by being allowed to table this statement. I think it will save the time of the committee if the statement were entered in Hansard. If not I shall proceed to put it in Hansard seriatim.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is not unanimous consent, the hon. member realizes he will have to read it. Is there unanimous consent?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman; I think the document should be read.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Then in connection with starred questions which I have put on the order paper and to which answers were given not in Hansard, but by an order for return, I should now like to put on Hansard the record of accidents of Autair Helicopter Services Limited on the continental polar shelf contract:
(a)	CF-KMV-Bell 47G2-ten miles from lake la Bouille, P.Q., on 25th February, 1959-the right ski sank in the snow on landing and the aircraft rolled over. Substantial damage.
(b)	CF-KMX-Bell 47G2-lake Gaillard, P.Q., on 7th March, 1959-while attempting take-off, the helicopter nosed over and crashed. Substantial damage.
(c)	CF-KMW-Alouette II-Labrieville south, Ber-simus 2, P.Q., on 13th May, 1959-on take-off, uncontrollable vibration attributed to ground resonance was set up and the aircraft crashed. Complete write-off.
(d)	CF-KMN-Bell 47G-northern Quebec on 10th July, 1959-the helicopter experienced a sudden loss of lift and crashed to the ground. Substantial damage.
(e)	CF-KMX-Bell 47G2-Veza lake, P.Q., on 15th January, 1960-while transporting an engine in a net slung beneath the helicopter, the net snagged in fallen trees during an approach to land. The aircraft tipped forward and crashed. Substantial damage.
(f)	CF-LME-Bell 47G2-Greening station, P.Q., on 10th March, 1960-the helicopter was parked close to the railway track and the rotor was struck by a passing train. Substantial damage.
(g)	CF-IKS-Bell 47G2-near Richmond gulf, P.Q., on 9th April, 1960-tiie helicopter experienced control difficulties during flight where the seizure of the lateral damper on the manual controls resulted in jamming of the cyclic stick which prevented the pilot from controlling the aircraft, which was forced landed. Substantial damage.
(h)	CF-IKR-Bell 47G2-de Gue river, P.Q., on 13th August, 1960-while attempting to land the
Supply-Transport
float equipped aircraft on a small sloping shelf of rock the aircraft toppled into the water. Substantial damage.
Then there is this note:
All involved partial write-off since major components were destroyed.
This is the record of the company to which the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys gave a contract for important helicopter services on the continental polar shelf. I asked what were the accidents in 1961 and I was told there were none. I have it from a reliable source that Bell 47G2A helicopter had an accident in 1961; tail boom extension smashed-

Mr. Chairman, it is all very well for the hon. member to talk about a very reliable source when reading a document. If he is going to read a document he should tell the committee what the document is, and if he wants to talk about a very reliable source he should not be afraid to name that source.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not speaking from a document; I have notes and I am making the statement in this committee that I was not given the information I should have been given in answer to this question. I have it on reliable information that there was an accident in 1961.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, what the hon. member for Laurier is stating in fact is that my department has not given a true answer to one of his questions. He is trying to prove that by saying to the committee, "I know from a very reliable source that the information given by the department was not true; it was not according to the facts." I think in all fairness, and according to the rules of the house, if the hon. member is going to make such a statement the least he could do is name that very reliable source.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know of any rule of the house whereby I am required to name the source.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I suggest-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just let me finish. The minister will have an opportunity to reply, and I hope he will give an explanation why it is that this accident of which I am about to give the details was not reported when I asked for the information.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the minister going to allow me-

-if the hon. member is speaking to the point of order I am ready to listen

to him, but if he is going to carry on from there without speaking to the point of order,
I think I have the right to continue.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the point of order on which the minister rose?

The point of order is that if an hon. member puts a question on the order paper or asks it on orders of the day and a minister files an answer, the hon. member has to accept that answer. What the hon. member for Laurier is now saying is, "Well, I have asked a question: were there any accidents reported to the department in 1961?", and he tells the committee that the department said there were no accidents. Then the hon. member says, "I have a very reliable source that says that the information given by the department is not according to the facts; it is not true". I think that is a serious accusation the hon. member is making, and the least he could do is tell the committee what his very reliable source is.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not making an accusation against-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just a moment. I am not making an accusation against the officers of the Department of Transport. I am making the statement that in 1961 there was an accident experienced by Autair Helicopter Services Limited, and in the information I have, that accident was not reported. Because of that I say that the officers of this department should now take the necessary steps to inquire whether or not it is a fact that Bell 47G2A helicopter had a tail boom extension smashed after being struck by its own main rotor blades, because of the lack of the pilot's experience, on the continental polar shelf project after the contract started, in 1961. That is what I am asking the minister to inquire into, and I am not accusing-
Would the hon. member give the date of this accident?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will have to give it to the minister later, just as the minister has not always at his finger tips all the information we request. But that is the point I am bringing to the attention of the minister. I think the minister should inquire whether or not that is the case, and if it is not the case and if I am wrong, I will rise in this house and apologize to the house for the statement which I have made.
I now move on to another part of the information that was given in connection with this matter. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, I advised the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys long before I rose to discuss this

matter that I intended to deal with it this evening. I spoke to him personally in the corridor, and I sent a message to his office.
It seems to me that part of this is not the responsibility of the Minister of Transport, but a great part of it is. That part which has to do with the air transport board falls under his jurisdiction, while that part which has to do with the giving of the contract is not his responsibility. I suggest that is why it is difficult to deal with a matter of this kind, two departments being involved. As the minister knows, in this case there are two departments involved.
It is well known that this firm is one which was very close to the late Premier Duplessis, and is equally close to the present federal government. Because of the statement which I have made I do not think the contract should have been given to that company under the circumstances it was given, by the filing of tariffs without the submission of tenders. I asked last year that this matter be investigated, but nothing was done. I have asked the minister again this year to make sure, before the contract was started upon, that the equipment which the minister listed to have been in possession of the contractor, was in his possession before he started to do the work on the continental polar shelf. From what was reported at the air industry transport association it appears that all the equipment which was required was not in the possession of that contractor and, in fact, that some of the equipment had to be obtained in the United States. That is why the resolution was passed at the air industry transport association protesting against allowing the equipment to be brought in from the United States under those circumstances. That resolution reads as follows:
Therefore be it resolved that the air transport board and the Department of Transport and the Department of National Revenue refuse to permit foreign-owned equipment to be imported under any lease or other short term device unless such suitable fixed or rotary wing aircraft cannot be procured from another Canadian operator at lease or charter rates and conditions considered fair and equitable by the air transport boar.
Be it further resolved, that in the allocation of government contracts priority be given to those operators equipped and qualified to perform the contract on which the tender is being submitted.
Mr. Chairman, I protest again the manner in which this operator was given the contract; that is, by the filing of tariffs on a second occasion.
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

If my memory serves me correctly this is the fifth time the hon. member

for Laurier has raised this matter in one form or another. I am becoming a little confused.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Laurier whether he is implying or alleging that in some way or another there exists mismanagement, there is patronage, there is collusion and there is inefficiency. Just exactly what is it that the hon. member is trying to prove?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suppose it does not matter very much how often I have raised this matter. I believe I am entitled to raise it a thousand times if I should want to. However, it is not the fifth time I have raised it but the third time.
I am complaining about the manner in which the contract was awarded. I am complaining about the fact that this company was refused a licence in the first instance by the air transport board. I am complaining about the fact that this company had its insurance cancelled twice, and I am complaining about the fact that it has had eight accidents of a serious nature, and that under the circumstances it should not have been entrusted with a contract of this kind in respect to the continental polar shelf.

May I ask the hon. member a question? In regard to the accidents which he has stated have taken place, could he explain to this committee where there has been any loss of life or any cost to the taxpayers?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There has been no loss of life but the accidents have entailed substantial damage in each case.
To whom?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To the aircraft; the helicopter.
What are you worried about?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not hear the question.
Are you worried about the company?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am worried about the fact that accidents of this kind are taking place up in the Arctic. I am worried about them because, if something is not done, one of these days someone will get killed and it will be too late.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 429 carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am interested in this problem because I have listened to the hon. member's statement regarding it on a number of occasions. He has convinced me that there is something wrong involved, and I am surprised that he should let the subject drop each time he makes his complaints. The
Business of the House
situation reminds me of one in which two individuals continually insult each other until they reach the stage of blows, at which time one sits down. I feel if what the hon. member for Laurier has said can be established by fact there is something seriously wrong with the licensing procedure of the department. I feel the charges which have been made by that hon. member are serious and, if untrue, should be answered by the minister. If the situation to which the hon. member has referred does exist, the minister should inform this committee what his department intends to do to correct that situation. I think the charges have been made with some justification because I have checked to the extent of meeting one of the officials of the company and have been informed that another tender was made. I suggest this is not a game that we are playing, and that at least some of the charges are accurate. Because of that, I feel the minister is obliged to inform this committee what is being done to terminate this problem. As the hon. member for Laurier pointed out, this awarding of the contract happened on two occasions under similar circumstances.
In view of the complexity of this problem, I am sure the minister wishes to reply, and I should, therefore, like to call it ten o'clock.

speechtext:
